about: The words of the cards of Data/encounters/rhine_frisia_793.json (the region rhine_frisia), with a picture line for each card (art.<card id>), four news items, and real words for the sixteen tollman.* keys of Data/writing.json (the card harbour.tollman.frankish), under the same keys. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite. Riddles said aloud are our own plain renderings of Symphosius (Riese 1894) and of Heidreks gátur 1, and (in the cards added 7 Oct 2026) of the Exeter Book's ship and ox, said as a boat mender and a tanner would have them at second hand; nothing is quoted from a modern translation. The words of the third batch of cards (the morning of 7 Oct 2026) follow those, with three more news items (the death of Godfred in 810, England after Cnut in 1036, Count Bruno's pennies): seven news items in all. Catla's words follow Rimbert c. 20 in our own wording; the old woman's oath at Doccinga follows the Utrecht Life of Boniface.

entries.text: The first question
The cargo is stowed and there is an hour of tide left. Ravn sits on the dam head with his feet over the water, and has a question for you.

Early evening on a timber dam head: a broad dark-bearded Northman sits with his feet over the brown river beside a small loaded boat, holding up one finger to the merchant; reed-roofed storehouses behind, the light low and yellow.
The boat's dry and the rope's new! So there's time, and I've remembered it. The question. The oldest one. A king was asked it in his own hall, and he didn't like it at all.
Here it is, then. What did I have yesterday that I want today? It harms men. It hinders words, and yet it rouses them. I'll not help you. I'd like to, mind.
Still chewing on it? Good. It's not a thing to chew. There, I've said too much.
You asked me to say it plainer, and I thought about it, and it was plain. A thing said plainer than that is only the answer.
You have it! I see it in how you sit. Oh, that's good, that's very good. It was on the bench in front of you all the time.
The priest calls this a fast day. Then it's a good day for this question, the best there is. A man knows best what he had when he hasn't got it, and I know it very well today.
Take the question away and think on it
Give him the answer
Ask him to say it plainer
The widow's storehouse
Thiadburg stands in the dark door of her storehouse with her ring of keys. Your goods are under her seal; she knows to the sack what is yours.

A broad timber storehouse on an earth dam, its door open on darkness and stacked bales: a grey-haired widow with a ring of keys at her belt stands in the doorway; on a high shelf behind her a small iron-bound chest; morning light, the river behind the viewer.
Your goods are dry and under my seal. I count when they come in and when they go out. Between the two nobody counts but me.
You. Good. Your corner is as you left it, and the mice have been spoken to.
Sit on that bale. There is a thing about this house you should hear from me and not from my brother.
The chest on the high shelf is for York. It holds less than the price. I know to the penny how much less.
It is paid. I slept the night through for the first time since my wedding.
I sell my grain for what it cost me and a penny. My brother keeps his doors shut and waits for Candlemas. We had the same mother. I have often wondered about it.
The Wōkerer has a stick with your name cut on it. If he asks me whether you are good for it, I shall tell him what I have seen and nothing else.
I have told the steward I stand for you. Do not make me a liar. I have never been one and I am too old to learn.
Hear what she has to tell about York
Ask her to stand for you before the steward
Buy two bolts of her blue cloth at a friend's price (84 d)
Thank her and see to the boat
Thiadbod's dam head
Thiadbod calls you up on to his own dam, where his big ship lies and his men are rolling casks. He is glad to see you. He is glad to see everyone.

A wide, well-kept dam head with a large round-hulled ship alongside: a stout smiling skipper in a good blue cloak beckons the merchant up a plank; behind him men roll wine casks into a storehouse; bright midday, gulls.
Neighbour! Come up, it is dry up here. They tell me you are going north by the Almere. No? You should. The cloth is good this year.
You said no last time and I respected it. I only ask again because the price has gone up.
Last time you asked what was in them. That was not neighbourly. But I am a neighbourly man.
A man called Eilbern lies at the eel stakes below Medemelacha. He has twelve bundles of mine and no boat free. Lie there one night. That is all the errand.
The toll is seen to. It always is. Twelve pennies now, for your trouble, and the rest is between you and the man on the Ems.
Say you will lie a night at the eel stakes
Ask what is in the bundles
Say your boat is too small to be worth his trouble
The king's mint
In the upper town a guard lets you into a low house that smells of charcoal. The moneyer does not look up from his pan; his clerk does.

A low dim workshop lit by a charcoal hearth: a stooped moneyer with burn-scarred forearms holds a small balance over a bench of dies and silver blanks; a young clerk with a wax tablet at his elbow; a spearman in the doorway against daylight.
Put it on the pan. All of it. I do not talk to silver in a purse.
You. Say what is in the purse before I weigh it, and I will tell you whether you know your own silver.
The king is making the penny heavier by a third. After Saint John's next the old ones go into my fire. I tell you before the dams hear it; make what you can of that.
Old pennies are silver now and nothing more. I take them by weight, less my cut. The toll man will not take them at all, and enjoys saying so.
That bag did not come out of a purse. It came out of the ground. Hearth ash on them, and salt. The island?
The island pennies ran better than I said they would. I do not often say that.
Three lines of Latin about what money was before it was money. Ten pennies. My master says it is a waste of wax, which is how I know it is good.
Bring me another of those with the writing like worms on a wet road. I will pay over the weight only to look at it.
Put the old pennies from the island in his fire
Buy the clerk's riddle (10 d)
Tell the clerk what money was
Have the purse weighed and say thank you
The letter from York
The poor sit along the wall of the upper church. The priest comes out to you with a letter in one hand and something wrapped in oiled hide under his arm.

A small timber church on a rise above two rivers: a thin tired priest in a worn brown habit holds out a wrapped book to the merchant; thin people sit along the church wall in the shade; far below, the comb of dams and a small boat; hot still afternoon.

A letter came from York. Heathen men have been at Saint Cuthbert's on the holy island: the altar dug up, brothers killed, boys carried off in the ships. I read it slowly. I read everything slowly. It did not get better.

It is a year since the holy island. They say the same ships came back for another house of monks this summer, and the sea took some of them at the river mouth. I do not know if that is justice. I am only a priest.
This book must go to the bishop's school at Traiectum. Half a day down the river. It is worth more than your boat and it must not get wet. I would take it myself, but look along my wall.
You said the hold was full. It is a small book.
Take the book, wrapped in oiled hide
Give a sack of rye for the people along his wall, and take the book
Say the hold is full
A plaint before the count's steward
A man of the count's meets you on the bank road: you are named in a plaint and the steward will hear it in the hall today. The count is away with the host.

A long timber hall, half empty, tally sticks hanging in bundles from the beams: a lean grey steward on a bench between the merchant and an angry barge skipper who points toward the river; a few bystanders; cool light from the open door.
A plaint. He says your boat lay across his posts in the night and his barge stove a plank against her. He asks twenty-four pennies. The count rides with the host, so you have me.
Ask anyone on the dam whose posts those are. My father drove them. I have the plank in the barge, if anybody wants to look at a plank.
The law of your people lets a man clear himself by his oath, with oath-helpers of his own standing. Your crew will do, if they look at me and not at their shoes.
Last time your helpers looked at their shoes. I remember shoes.
You cleared yourself before me once already. Do not make a custom of needing to.
Clear yourself by oath, with your crew as oath-helpers
Pay him the twenty-four pennies and have done
Offer to mend his plank with your own hands, and stand him ale
The breaking beach
Old hulls lie on the mud above the tide line, half taken apart. The wright walks round your boat once before he says anything.

A muddy river beach with two old clinker hulls being broken up for their planks: a slow broad shipwright with an adze over his shoulder looks along the keel of the merchant's small boat; a boy of fourteen coils rope nearby; grey morning, wood smoke.
She is sound. Whoever built her knew where to stop. I would have put one more rib aft, but I was not asked.
The oak. Did you bring it, or did you bring a story about it?
I want oak from up the river: long, straight, split and not sawn. Four loads before the frost. Nobody downriver has a tree worth the name.
My sister's boy wants the water. He can bail, splice and keep quiet. Two of those are rare.
I can keep quiet.
Take his order: four loads of oak before the frost
Take the boy aboard
Talk about the boat and promise nothing
The black-haired merchant
Behind the bank road a man with black hair going grey sits among cakes of wax the colour of butter. He names a price before you have asked one.

A lean-to shop in a row of workshops: a black-haired, sharp-faced merchant in a good dark tunic sits behind stacked round cakes of yellow wax with a hand on a covered balance; the merchant stands in the lane; dusty afternoon light.
Wax. Clean, the colour of butter. Thirty pennies the cake, and I am robbing myself. The church pays forty and complains.
You are the small boat off the widow's dam. I know every hull on this bank. I do not lodge them. A man who lodges guests ends by feeding poets.
You weighed it. Nobody weighs it. Very well: for you the true cakes, and we say no more about it.
The prior at Traiectum is a suspicious old man. Do not let him tell you things about my wax.
Buy two cakes at thirty
Put the cakes on your own scale first, then buy two
Say the church can have it
Aldswith's bench
Aldswith's house is full of crews waiting on a cargo or a wind. She looks at your men, then at you, and holds out her hand before anyone sits.

A smoky hall-house crowded with boatmen on benches round a long hearth: a strong grey-eyed ale-wife with a jug stands before the merchant, palm out; a dark-bearded Northman sits alone by the door post; evening, firelight.

I had my letters at Saint Martin's, and this with them, for eight pennies: two iron points joined in one. I fight the wind and the deep water. I search the middle of the stream, and I bite the land itself.
Pay for the crew before they drink, shipman. We talk after.
Your men drank what you paid for and one cup more. I let the one go. I do not let two go.
Offa dead? Who sold you that, and what did you pay for it? A cloth man was in from Lundenwic at Pentecost and cursed him by name, alive.
No grain boat has reached the terps since Easter. A man in from Doccinga says a sack of rye buys cloth there, and nobody haggles.
Thiadbod's steersman sat where you are sitting and said 'wine' twice in one breath. Men who are carrying wine say it once.
My brother at the toll says a boat that tells the truth three times is waved through the fourth. He has never yet waved one through.
Pay the crew's score and sit (4 d)
Ask her more about the terps and the rye
Buy the schoolboy's riddle (8 d)
Sit by the door post and listen
A burying at De Heul
A bier is carried along the bank road to the graves at De Heul: an old skipper of the dams, dead in his bed, which the bank finds remarkable.

A low sandy rise with rows of graves and a few wooden posts: four boatmen carry a bier with a coffin of dark old boat planks; a priest walks ahead, a small upright widow behind with a coil of rope over her arm; flat grey light, the river beyond.
He sailed forty summers and drowned in none of them. Carry him the last furlong, somebody who knows what a load is.
He said the boat was to be broken and the planks laid round him. The priest says a coffin is a coffin. So he lies in his own strakes.
There is his rope and his second sail. I cannot eat them.
The ground is hard. We have been digging since first light.
Take a corner of the bier and give for the Mass (6 d)
Buy his rope and sail from her at an honest price (46 d)
Stand at the back with your head bare
A feast day at midsummer
Ash from the midsummer fires still lies along the dams, and nobody is selling. The church's bell is a board struck with a mallet, and it is being struck.

The long row of dams on a bright midsummer morning, empty stalls and heaps of grey ash from bonfires: people in their best cloaks walk up toward a small church on the rise; a priest at the roadside; a dark-bearded Northman leaning on a post watching.
No selling till the Mass is said. The Lord's saints are owed a morning. They ask no toll on the afternoon.
Pray for the brothers of the holy island. It is not three weeks since they were keeping their own saint's peace.
They lit fires on the dams at midsummer for their saint. At home we light them the same night for no saint. The fire does not ask.
Keep the feast: Mass, then meat and ale for the crew (8 d)
Load quietly behind the storehouse while the dams are at Mass
Let the crew go up to the church and keep the boat yourself
The salter on the dams
Between two dams a man from the coast has grey salt heaped on a hide and a wax tablet stuck in his belt, which is not usual in a salter.

A gap between two timber dams with small boats: a soot-dark coast salter sits by a heap of coarse grey salt on a hide with a wooden scoop, a wax tablet tucked in his belt; a housewife bargains; behind, masts and reed roofs; noon glare.
Marsh salt. Grey, and it bites. Three pennies the sack here, and I carried it up the river myself.
A monk bought salt of me for his abbey and paid part in this. Latin. He said it over till I had it. I was water once, and swam with the fish. Fire changed me. Now I am white as ash and snow.
Twelve pennies for the tablet and the saying of it. The monk said it is the first of a longer road. He did not say where the road goes.
So it is my own goods I have been saying over all these years. The monk might have told me.
You bought of me before. Then the last lot kept your fish.
Buy two sacks of his salt (6 d)
Buy the tablet and the saying of it (12 d)
Taste a grain and walk on
The school house
Boys' voices chanting one line over and over stop when you darken the door. The master sends them out with a look and turns to you.

A plain timber room against a pale stone wall: benches, wax tablets, a great iron-bound chest; a tall stooped schoolmaster with ink on his fingers faces the merchant in the doorway while small boys squeeze out past him; slanting morning light and dust.
A shipman at the school door. Either you have a book or you have lost a boy. Which?
Alfward's book. Give it here. No: wipe your hands, then give it here.
Your book is read aloud at supper. The boys complain that it is long. That is how I know it is good.
I set every new boy the same three lines. I bring great strength out of a small body. I open what is shut, and shut what is open. I keep the house for its master, and he keeps me. Well?
A key. Yes. A boy of nine had it before you did, but he had seen fewer locks.
You know now what a book is. Forty calves, a year of a man's eyes, and one wet night undoes it.
Liudger carried the best of that chest home from York in a merchant's hull, with every Frisian in the city running for the ships. I stayed here and kept the door. Somebody must.
Hand over the book from Dorestat
Take his three lines away to think on
Answer the three lines
Leave him to his boys
The prior's store
An old monk with a ring of keys sits on a cask at the store door, where he can see the gate, the guest house and you.

A stone-footed storehouse inside an old fort wall: a very old, small, upright monk sits on a cask in the doorway with keys in his lap and a balance hanging from the lintel; sacks and wax cakes in the dark behind; clear noon light.
I am the prior. I keep the gate, the store and the porridge. Four masters of this house have eaten my porridge and three of them are dead. I draw no conclusion.
Butter-coloured cakes. I know those cakes. Put one on my scale before you name a price.
The black-haired man's wax, at the black-haired man's weight. I paid you for what was there. I wrote down what was not.
You praised the porridge. I have told the bishop. He did not believe me.
The king says the bishop is to feed the hungry till harvest. The king did not send the grain. They are at my gate every morning, and I have counted the sacks twice.
Frisia gives no oil and no wine. A poet said so, in this house, with his mouth full of my butter.
Sell him two cakes of wax on his own scale (36 d the cake)
Sell him the two butter-coloured cakes, for what they weigh
Sell four sacks of rye at the price he can pay (3 d the sack)
Eat at the guest table and praise the porridge
The bishop's hall
The bishop receives you standing, with a deacon at a writing board beside him. Everything said here is written down, and both of them know it.

A timber hall built against a Roman stone wall: a careful, formal bishop of about fifty in a plain dark cloak with a silver cross stands before a chair; a deacon writes at a sloping board; the merchant bare-headed before them; even indoor light.
You stand in Saint Willibrord's house. Say your business slowly. My deacon writes slowly.
A letter from Liudbod at Daventre. I can tell you what it says before the seal is broken: the rope is ready, send the bell.
I have no bell to spare. I have bronze, if someone will pay the founder. Tell Liudbod so, gently.
My prior speaks of your house without sighing. That is rare, and I have had it noted.
The count's steward counts Saint Martin's tenth at Dorestat as if it were his own teeth. I should not mind standing between him and an honest house, once.
Saint Martin's wants wax before Candlemas. Six cakes, true weight. I pay on the day.
Give him the letter from Daventre
Ask him to stand surety for you on the Wōkerer's day
Take his order: six cakes of wax
Ask his blessing on the boat and go
A priest for the Ems
On the strand under the wall a young priest sits on a small chest, holding a bell wrapped in a cloak and watching the boats as a man watches horses he must ride.

A muddy river strand under a pale old fort wall, boats drawn up: a thin young priest sits stiffly on a chest hugging a cloak-wrapped bell; a broad ferryman leans on a pole beside him, amused; the merchant's small boat in the foreground; mild spring light.
That is the bishop's young man for the Ems mouth. He has a chalice, a book and a small bell, and he asked me which end of a boat goes first.
Liudger has asked for a priest. I am the priest. I am told it is the Vecht, then the Almere, then the coast, and that I should not look at the water.
They say your boat brought a priest out of that country when it burned. Then you know the way back.
He is still here. He has learned to sit in a boat that is tied up.
Give him passage to Emuthon
Take him, and ask the bishop's house for his passage (20 d)
Say you are bound the other way
The long fast
The guest table is laid with porridge, beans and small ale. Your crew look at it and then at you.

A long plank table in a bare guest house: wooden bowls of grey porridge and beans, one small smoked fish on a board; an elderly monk stands with folded hands at the head; four boatmen on the bench looking glum; thin Lenten daylight through a doorway.
It is the long fast. In this house that is porridge, beans, and a herring looked at from a distance. Your men may eat as we eat, or eat on their boat.
The eel is a fish, thank God, and the Vecht is full of them. The woman on the levee smokes them. I have never said so to her face.
There was a smell of pork on the strand last Lent. I name no boat.
You kept the fast with us last year, and your men did not die of it. I had wondered.
Keep the fast with the house
Buy smoked eels from the alehouse for the crew (4 d)
Open the salt pork aboard, out of sight
Hildeburg's alehouse
On the levee a widow is turning eels on a rack over a slow fire. She counts your crew as they come up the bank, and finds the number short.

A turf-walled alehouse on a river levee with a smoking rack of eels outside: a brisk widow of about fifty with her sleeves rolled points a fish-knife at a lanky young boatman sitting on an upturned logboat; the fort wall behind; late afternoon.
You are a man short. I counted your crew as they came up the bank. I count everybody.
That one by the eel rack is a boatman's son with no boat. He poles, he can splice, and he owes me for the winter. Take him, and his first wages come to me.
I know the Vecht to the Almere and the Almere to the stream at Medemelacha. Past that I know what I am told.
How is my boatman? Alive? Then you owe me nothing and he owes me less.
Hire him for the season
Drink her ale and hear the strand's news (2 d)
Say the men you have are enough for this boat
The crossing at the Vecht mouth
Where the Vecht leaves the Rhine a man is hollowing an oak into a boat. He goes on working while he talks.

A river fork with reed beds: a broad, quiet ferryman stands knee-deep in wood chips inside a half-hollowed oak trunk on trestles, adze in hand; his ferry punt tied to a post; the narrow Vecht winding north into reeds; hazy light.
North by the Vecht it is a day to the Almere, if you know which reeds are bank and which are only reeds.
I will take you through for six pennies. Or bring me two loads of Rhineland oak, long and straight, and I will show you the marks and you need never pay me again. I am a fool about oak.
You sat on my mud a whole tide last time. I waved. It seemed polite.
Pay him six pennies to take her through
Give him two loads of oak for the marks
Pole it yourself and trust the reeds
Saint Martin's
The church is one stone room, cold and bright with lamps. A priest with a key on a cord round his neck stands by the treasure chest behind the altar.

The inside of a small stone church: an altar with a few lamps, an open iron-bound chest showing silver vessels, one a low cup with a band of interlaced beasts; a priest holding a key on a cord; the merchant with his cap in his hand; lamplight and deep shadow.
The plate is shown to those who give. Give first.
This is Saint Martin's month. He cut his cloak in two for a beggar. The toll men of the north are at the guest table with the bishop's tenth, and they have cut nothing in two.
An old cup with beasts under the rim, biting their own backs? There is one. It came from the north in my master's time. Nobody wrote down where.
You looked a long time at the cup with the beasts. Most men look at the gold one.
Give alms and see the plate (4 d)
Give alms, and look for the old man's cup (4 d)
Offer a cake of wax at the altar
Hear Mass and keep your purse shut
A promise at the old minster
At the old minster a canon is watching the river over the wall, not the altar. When he hears a boat is in he comes down to the strand himself.

The top of an old Roman fort wall at dusk: an old canon in a dark cloak shades his eyes down the wide river; below, the strand, a few boats and the merchant looking up; far downstream a line of small square sails.
Sails went by under this wall for Dorestat and did not stop. One summer they will stop. So I ask every skipper I trust for one promise.
If the bishop must leave, there is a chest: the school's books and the altar things. There will be more chests than boats. Promise me yours.
You swore. I have told Saint Salvator, who forgets nothing, and the prior, who forgets less.
They came while the Dane who holds Dorestat was away in his own country. The bishop goes up the river today. The chest is on the bank. Now, shipman.
Your house swore to this before the altar. I was not the one who heard it. It is written down, and I can read.
Swear it before the altar
Take the chest aboard for Daventre
Give for the lamp and promise nothing (3 d)
Say a small boat can promise nothing
Our own fire
The merchants of the Stathe are standing in their own street with torches. The sails that burned Tiel last year are on the Lek.

A street of timber merchants' houses outside a town wall at dusk: a grey-bearded merchant in a good cloak holds a lit torch and looks back over his shoulder at the viewer; behind him men carry bales through a gate; far off on the river, sails.
Tiel burned last year. My cousin came up the river with a scale, a wife and nothing else. Now the same sails are on the Lek.
Nothing left outside the wall, we say. Nothing for them to sit in, and nothing to burn that we have not burned ourselves. I have the first torch. I am looking for the second.
Take the second torch
Carry the street's goods inside the wall first
Get your own goods aboard and lie off in the stream
The clerks' bench
In a lean-to against the palace wall a clerk sits among wax tablets and charter chests with nobody to talk to but masons. He looks up as a starving man looks at bread.

A lean-to of new timber against a half-built stone palace wall: a quick, vain young clerk with ink-stained fingers holds out a wax tablet across a bench stacked with tablets and rolled parchments; scaffolding and a stone-cutter behind; bright cold light.
A face that is not a mason's. Sit. Do you read? No. Does anyone on your boat read? I ask everyone. One day the answer will be yes.

Three lines on wax. There is a house on the earth that sounds with a clear voice. The house is loud; the guest in it is silent. Yet both run on together, the guest and the house. Take it. Bring it back answered.
The river and the fish. My master set it to the king's son Pippin, who was a boy, and the boy had it at once. I was sixteen and did not.
They say the English have the same riddle in their own tongue. If you ever hold it, bring it here. I would give a good deal to see how that tongue manages 'guest'.
My master is abbot at Tours now. He still writes. I read the letters to the cellarer, who listens like a cask.
Take the wax tablet
Give him the answer
Show him the English riddle of the fish and the river
Tell him the news of the river and go
The king's cellar
The cellar is cut into the hill under the palace: cool, dark and half empty. Its keeper lifts a sack to feel the weight before he greets you.

A vaulted cellar of old Roman stone with rows of casks, hanging hams and stacked sacks: a broad bald cellarer with a ring of iron keys and a bundle of tally sticks hefts a sack in both arms; the merchant in the doorway against daylight.
What have you got, what does it weigh, and is it the king's measure or your own?
Einbert's hooks and knives. He sent them by a merchant, so he means to be paid this time. Clever. Put them there.
Tell the smith he has his silver and I have his nails, and that neither of us enjoyed it.
Your count eats here when the king keeps a feast. He likes a hound that will hold a boar, a salmon in a fast, and good Rhine wine. Nothing that looks like payment.
The court may come this year or in ten. The cellar must be full a month before, and not a day sooner.
Hand over the smith's three crates and take his silver
Take his order: six casks of Rhine wine
Let him lift a sack, and say nothing
The count at the king's table
It is a feast, and the palace hall is full of lords and their men. Your count is on a bench among them with a cup in his hand. He has seen you.

A long stone hall by rushlight, benches of Frankish lords in bright cloaks: a thick-set count in a red cloak turns on his bench, cup in hand, to look down at the merchant who stands before him; hounds under the tables; smoke and gold light.
The shipman from my own dams. You have come a long way up a brown river to find me with a cup in my hand.
Those are English hounds. Do not tell me what they cost. Tell me whether they hold.
The boar this morning was as long as a bench. Ask me for something before I remember who I am.
Before these lords I cannot refuse a gift and I cannot be seen to take a payment. You have chosen your day well, or someone chose it for you.
Give him a hound, and ask for time
Send two casks of Rhine wine to his table, and ask for time
Ask for an errand in place of part of the silver
Bow, and say nothing of the debt
The huntsman at the gate
A silent man in green and brown stands at the fort gate with two hounds on one leash. He lets three masons pass, and stops you.

The gate of an old stone fort on a wooded hill: a lean silent Saxon huntsman in a hooded green cloak, a boar spear in one hand and two hounds on a leash, blocks the path of the merchant; oak woods behind; grey morning mist.
You go by the IJssel, they say. There is an ale-wife at Daventre, a Saxon. She passes word between those of us carried west and those left at home.
Tell her the man from the king's wood is alive, eats, and has been taught his prayers a second time. She will know which man.
Did she pour before she asked, or ask before she poured? If she asked first, she is well.
The count hunts here on feast days. When the boar is good he gives things away. I find the boar.
Carry his word to Daventre
Ask him to send word when the hunt has gone well
Buy a haunch for the crew, and ask no questions (5 d)
Nod and go in
Forty on the road
By the old graves below the church people are sitting who belong to no lord: thin, quiet, with their bundles beside them. The priest is among them with an empty basket.

A roadside below a small church on a hill, old stone grave-markers in the grass: some forty thin people with bundles sit in the dusk; a tired kind priest with an empty basket stands among them looking toward the merchant; smoke of one small fire.
I ask for nothing. I say only that the road has no lord, and there are forty on it by the old graves tonight.
In Lent the king had a law written on this hill: who buys at harvest for two to sell at six takes shameful gain. It was read out at the gate. The forty did not come up to hear it.
They ate. Two have gone on toward Colonia. One has gone further than that; I buried him on the third day.
Give two sacks of rye at the church door
Sell him two sacks at the lawful price (8 d)
Say your hold is the count's before it is yours
What the palace hears
A clerk of the palace comes down the hill path to the landing before your rope is fast. Somebody up there counts boats.

A shelving river landing under a steep wooded hill with palace walls on the skyline: a palace clerk in a long tunic hurries down the path toward a small boat making fast; downstream, low on the horizon, a smear of smoke; overcast.
From the count of Walcheren. Again. I can say it without reading it: forty spears, no wall, send ships.
The emperor is bound for Rome this year. Ships have been ordered. They are always being ordered.
The emperor Lothar is in the fort. That smoke downriver is Dorestat. He has men. He is not moving, and nobody here will say why aloud.
Boats came up at first light with burned people in them. The cellar is feeding them. That much we can do.
Give him the count's word, and say what you saw yourself
Carry burned people on up the river, for nothing
Say nothing and look at the river
Hathugard's question
The ale-wife on the bank has the jug in her hand, and does not pour. She looks at each of you in turn, and then asks.

A low thatched alehouse on a river bank, a ferry and a wooden church behind: a straight-backed Saxon woman of fifty holds a jug without pouring and looks hard at the merchant; a big silent mate sits on the bench staring at his hands; dusk.
Before I pour. Have you seen a Saxon of about thirty, with a scar through the left eyebrow from a calf's kick? He was thirteen when they counted him off. He answers to Brunric, or did.
You said you would ask along the Rhine. I do not ask what you heard. I ask whether you asked.
You have a word for me from the west. I can see it on you. A man carries a message as he carries a full cup.
Sit. For once I pour first.
The count's men drink here in May, and pay. I serve them at a fair price. I have never said I forgave anybody.
Promise to ask along the Rhine
Give her the huntsman's word from Noviomagus
Say you have seen no such man, and drink
The host's ground
The meadow below the church is trodden to mud and full of carts. A man with a bundle of tally sticks walks straight to your boat.

A trampled river meadow crowded with ox-carts, tethered horses and tents, a wooden church on a dune behind: a brisk Frankish quartermaster with tally sticks in his belt points at the merchant's hold; a big Saxon mate turns his back; windy spring day.
The host crosses here when the grass is up. I buy oats, salt pork and anything on four legs. I pay the count's price, on a stick, and the stick is paid at Michaelmas. Usually.
My village fed this host once. Nobody asked the village.
Your pork marched to the Weser. I did not hear it complain.
This year the king's ships go overland into Saxony. Do not ask me how. I buy rope.
Sell him two barrels of salt pork at the count's price
Take his order: eight sacks of oats within the month
Say the boat is bespoke
North of the grave, south of the grave
Mass is about to be said over Lebuin's grave. The Saxons stand to the north of it and the soldiers to the south, and there is room on both sides.

The inside of a small plank church with a grave-slab in the floor: on one side plainly dressed Saxon farmers, on the other Frankish soldiers with their helmets under their arms; a patient priest between them at the altar; a new rope hanging from the roof with no bell on it.
At Mass the Saxons stand north of Lebuin's grave and the soldiers south. I say one Mass for both, and God sorts it.
I call them with a soldier's shout. I want a bell. The rope is plaited and hung. Carry a letter to the bishop for me: the rope is ready, send the bell.
No bell to spare, but bronze, if someone will pay the founder. That is a bishop's yes. I have had worse.
Listen. No, wait for the hour. There. The soldiers cross themselves and the Saxons look up. It is the same bell for both.
You have been up the Heest. People come down from that hill looking at their feet. What did you see?
The crock is gone from the hollow, and a new one is there. I did not think it would be otherwise.
Take his letter for the bishop
Pay toward the founding of the bell (60 d)
Tell him what is in the hollow on the Heest
Hear Mass, and stand where there is room
The hollow on the Heest
You climb the Heest for a look at the river. Under an old thorn there is a hollow, a crock, rags tied in the branches and a ring of ash. A woman is setting down a comb of honey.

A wooded hill above a wide river: under a twisted thorn hung with faded rags, a clay crock in a hollow and a ring of ash; a farm woman in a decent headcloth kneels with a honeycomb on a leaf and looks up, caught; green shade, evening.
You did not see me. I did not see you. That is how it is done on this hill.
My man stands south of the grave on Sundays, with the soldiers. I stand there too. The bees are mine.
It is only honey. If there is nobody there to take it, where is the harm? And if there is, I had rather be on the right side of him.
Leave a penny in the crock
Say nothing, and go down
Sign yourself, and tell her the priest should hear of it
Heath iron
The forge stands open to the bank so that the smith can see who lands. He looks at your hands before your face.

An open-sided forge on a river bank: a proud, heavy-armed Frankish smith at the anvil, bars of dark heath iron stacked by the post, three nailed crates by the door; he squints at the merchant's hands; sparks, grey sky, the ferry beyond.
Show me your hands. Rope and oar. Good. I do not sell to men with soft hands; they come back to complain.
The keeper of the king's larder at Noviomagus ordered hooks, knives and nails, and pays late when he pays. Three crates. Put them in his hand and bring me what he gives. A fifth of it is yours.
You have been to the palace. I can hear silver in a man's walk.
Eighty-four pennies of mine went down the river in your purse. I have told the ferryman, and the ferryman tells everyone who crosses.
A man who brings back another man's silver buys rivets at my price, not the bank's.
Take the three crates for Noviomagus
Give him his silver, less your fifth (67 d)
Tell him the cellarer has not paid yet
Watch him draw a bar, and buy nothing today
The chest at Lebuin's church
Clerks of Saint Martin's are waiting on the bank at Daventre. They have been waiting some days, and they count your crew before they count the chest.

A river bank below a wooden church on a dune: three anxious clerics lift a heavy iron-bound chest out of a small boat; one holds the lid open and writes on its inside with a pen; a bell wrapped in a cloak on the grass; clear cold morning.
The bishop is given a house far up the Maas for now. But the chest comes here, to Lebuin, where there are walls of a sort and no sea.
We count it in front of you. Eleven books, the altar silver, a bell wrapped in a cloak. Nothing is wet. I did not expect that.
The name of your house goes on the inside of the lid, in ink. Lids outlast bishops.
Hand it over and ask nothing
Hand it over and name the freight (120 d)
Keep back one book against the freight
News at Wiltrud's house
At Wiltrud's fire a skipper nobody knows is telling the bench something for the third time, louder each time. He sees a new face and begins again.

A low oak-built house behind the dunes, a peat fire and benches of waiting skippers: a red-faced stranger stands with a cup raised, mid-speech; a dry, watchful ale-wife behind him catches the merchant's eye and very slightly shakes her head; night, firelight.
Offa is dead. The English king. I had it from a man who had it from a monk. The ports will open by the next moon, and they will be begging for black stones on the Strand.
Stand me a cup for it. News like that is worth a cask.
He told it at Easter too. And the Easter before. One year he will be right, and there will be no living with him.
You paid for his cup last time. He has been killing kings on the strength of it ever since.
Pay his score and thank him (3 d)
Buy two pair of quernstones on the strength of it (20 d)
Ask Wiltrud what she thinks of it
The old pennies
At the brooch-maker's hearth a woman is holding out a handful of small thick pennies as if they had gone bad. The brooch-maker takes one and rings it on his stone.

A smith's hearth in a narrow oak house: a quick-handed brooch-maker rings a tiny thick coin on an anvil stone, head cocked; a marsh woman holds a clay pot of the same coins in both hands; moulds and half-made brooches on the bench; side light from a shutter.
The steward cried it on the street: the new penny and no other. I have a pot of my grandmother's. What am I to do with them, eat them?
Ring it on the stone. Hear that? Silver. This one is half copper: it sings flat. The bite of a file tells you the rest.
I buy them for the melt at a brooch-maker's price. The mint gives more and takes its cut. The Danes at Ripa put them on the scale and ask nothing. Three reckonings. Pick one.
You paid the last woman fairly. My sister says so, and my sister says very little that is kind.
Buy the pot by weight, fairly (30 d)
Tell her they are dead coin, and offer fifteen
Sit with him an afternoon and learn the ring of good silver
The count's word
The count of the island is in the king's house with a Dane in the emperor's pay beside him. Both look tired. The count speaks before you have crossed the floor.

A plain oak hall on an island of dunes: a heavy-shouldered Frankish count in a mail shirt and faded red cloak leans on a table; beside him a tall fair Dane with a cross at his neck, arms folded; spears stacked by the door; wind, grey light through the smoke-hole.
You came down the river. What did you see on it? Ships, I mean. Not yours.
Witla is ash. The town on the Scheldt is ash. I have forty spears and an island of shepherds.
They will come on a morning flood with the wind behind them. It is what I would do.
Carry my word to the palace at Noviomagus: the island cannot be held without ships. I have sent it before. They may believe a merchant's eyes.
Carry his word to Noviomagus
Sell the watch a coil of rope, and wish him luck
Tell him what you saw, and sail on the ebb
The side room
Bernhild sells cheese at the marsh edge with sixty ewes behind her. She buys honey and linen with the silver, and does not eat the one or wear the other.

A turf-walled farmhouse on a flat salt marsh dotted with sheep: a weathered straight-backed woman in a grey gown stands by a rack of round cheeses; behind her the house's one shuttered side door; a huge pale sky.
Cheese is four pennies the wheel, and I do not come down. Wool after shearing.
Honey I buy, and linen, the cleanest you have. Do not ask me who for.
Wiltrud told you. She tells everyone, and then tells them not to say. My sister has not left the side room in eleven years. Her face. That is all there is to know.
That smell. Marsh herbs and mutton fat. The wise woman on the Ems sent me the making of it once, by word of mouth, and I never got it right.
It eases. It does not mend. She said it would not. Thiadwih slept through two nights.
Give her the salve from the Ems, and say it will not mend
Give her a crock of honey and take no silver
Buy two wheels of cheese (8 d)
Ask who the linen is for
The salt hearths
Out on the marsh, low smoke lies over a row of clay hearths. Men black to the elbows are raking grey ash, and one of them straightens up as you come.

A flat tidal marsh in autumn: a row of clay hearths with lead pans steaming, heaps of cut peat and grey ash; a salter black with soot leans on a wooden rake beside filled sacks; a small boat on the creek mud; low sun through smoke.
We burn the peat, wash the ash and boil what runs out. It is grey and it bites. The white salt from the south costs three times as much and salts no better.
At the hearth it is two pennies the sack. On the street it is three, and at Dorestat four. You have a boat. Do the reckoning.
You came back. Then the last lot kept your fish.
The lord in the hall is a Dane now. He takes his gift in salt, and counts sacks like a Frisian.
Buy six sacks at the hearth (12 d)
Lend your crew to carry peat for a day, and take salt for it
Taste it, nod, and walk on
The pilot's shed
The old pilot sits on a pile of nets in his shed door, looking at the bar. He knows who you are by your boat before he has looked at you.

A net shed on a marsh ridge above a wide grey river mouth: a wiry white-stubbled old pilot in a salt-stiff hooded cloak sits on heaped nets, a sounding pole taller than himself against the wall; a boy of eight coiling a lead-line; the white line of the bar far out.
You came over the bar on the last of the ebb with a hand's breadth under you. I watched. Do not do it again.
Thiadbod's ship is looked for. Until she is in I take nobody over. He pays me by the year for that. I never said I liked it.
You asked about the water and not about my price. Few do. She runs north of the bank since the floods.
Come out at the spring ebb. I will show you the marks once. My daughter's boy will check you; he has better eyes and worse manners.
You have the marks. Keep them in your head. A thing that is written down can be sold.
Sit on the net pile and ask him about the water
Go out with him at the spring ebb
Pay him double to take you over now (12 d)
Wait a tide
Five cows for Ganda
At the abbey's farm behind the strand a woman is weaving in the open door with five thin cows in the yard. She stops the loom when she sees what kind of boat you have.

A small farmstead on a marsh ridge: a lean capable woman at an upright loom in a doorway, grey-blue cloth half woven; five thin cows and a girl of ten in the yard; a hungry summer, brown grass, heat haze over the river mouth.
The farm is Saint Peter's of Ganda. Five cows, four of us, and a bolt of cloth and the cheeses owed each year whether there is bread or not.
We have eaten the seed barley. My own bolt I will give for bread. The abbey's bolt I will not touch.
My daughter's freedom is written on a scrap in the roof. I have the price put by, less eleven pennies. Barley stands between the eleven and nothing.
You sold at the king's price when the strand was asking ten. The priest said your name from the cross. I did not need telling.
Sell four sacks of rye at the king's price, paid in cheese
Take her own bolt of cloth for four sacks: the strand's price
Give her the eleven pennies
Say you have no grain to spare
Dice at Wilsuit's
Three skippers are waiting on a wind at Wilsuit's, and one of them is rattling bones in a horn cup. He pushes a stool out with his foot.

A cramped alehouse on a strand: a cheerful loud skipper shakes a horn cup of bone dice over an upturned cask, a stool pushed out for the viewer; behind him a watchful ale-wife counting on her fingers; a shutter banging in the wind, rushlight.
Waiting on a wind? So am I. Ten pennies on three bones. I lose calmly and I win loudly; you have been warned of both.
He pays his score once a year, in cloth, and thinks I do not know where the cloth comes from.
You took ten pennies off me. I have told the whole strand it was twenty. A man must lose well.
Your ten pennies bought a round. The strand drank your health. You were not there.
I mean to be first over the water after any bad news. That is when prices are stupid.
Throw the bones with him (10 d)
Stand him a cup and ask what he saw over the water (2 d)
Watch the bones and keep your purse shut
The eel stakes
You lie the night among the eel stakes below the row. Some time after the moon is down a boat comes alongside without a light, and a man speaks low.

Black night on still inland water among rows of thin stakes: two small boats side by side, a man passing a long wrapped bundle across by feel; a single far-off hearth glow on the low shore; stars, no moon.
No light. Hold her off with the oar. Twelve bundles, an arm long, heavier than they look. They go on to the Ems mouth, to a man called Folcger at the creek.
Do not ask me to open one. I have carried them four years and never opened one. That is what I am paid for.
The toll man counts hulls at first light and looks at waterlines. He has never caught me. He has never stopped looking.
My aunt owns half this boat. If you speak to her, we met about eels.
Take the twelve bundles aboard
Go to the toll man at first light and tell him
Push off and leave him his bundles
The marks on the door post
The house where skippers sleep has a door post dark with handling, cut from knee to shoulder with marks and notches. The woman of the house has a knife in her hand.

The doorway of a thatched house on a peat stream: a strong plain widow with a small knife cuts a notch in a door post covered with carved owners' marks and rows of notches; boatmen's shoes in a row by the threshold; warm hearth light from inside, dusk outside.
What is your boat's mark? I cut it in the door post, so that I know whose shoes to throw out.
Your mark is on the post with a notch beside it. A notch for each time a man comes back. Some have a long row. Some have a line cut through.
Four notches. Your place on the bench is kept. So I will tell you what I would not tell a new boat.
Eight. The toll man nods to you before he counts your hull. He has nodded to six men in twenty years.
That mark, low down, worn pale. You have his walk. Sit where he sat.
I have heard what you carried to the Ems. My sister's son will hang one day for a fat man's silver. Do you mean to be standing beside him?
Give her your mark, and pay for the bench (3 d)
Ask what she would not tell a new boat
Sleep aboard
The stone ground
Behind the row a man sits in grey dust among black stones, knocking on each with his knuckle and listening. He is a little deaf, and shouts.

A yard behind thatched houses strewn with dark porous quernstones and grey chippings: a half-deaf craftsman covered in stone dust holds a pick in one hand and raps a stone with the knuckles of the other, ear cocked; stacked finished pairs in straw; flat noon light.
Speak up. Twenty years of the pick. I hear stones better than men.
Knock on it. A sound stone rings. A cracked one says 'tock', like a lie.
The English shore is shut, and I have two summers' stones in the nettles. The reeve over there has never seen my face, and he has cost me a cow.
Bring me roughouts from Colonia. Sound ones, not the ones the dealers keep for Frisians. Four pair, and I pay over the bank's price.
Take his order: four pair of sound roughouts
Buy a dressed pair he has kept back (10 d)
Knock on a stone, listen, and learn what 'tock' sounds like
The bare mound
On the second mound a square of grass is left ungrazed. A very old man with a herdsman's staff stands at its edge, and moves to keep you off it.

A low house mound in a huge flat salt marsh: an ancient herdsman with a long staff stands guard at the edge of a bare square of longer grass; sheep graze everywhere but there; six other mounds with thatched roofs in a row behind; high cloud, wind.
Keep off that square of grass. The sheep know. You can learn.

I was a boy when the Franks burned what stood there. We set the posts up again. I was past fifty when the priest's men came in a boat and broke it for good, and weighed the silver on the grass. Two parts for the king, one for the priest.
I do not want it back. I want to know where it went. They say Saint Martin's at Traiectum shows its plate to a man who gives alms. Look for a cup with beasts under the rim, biting their own backs.
You have been to Traiectum. You have the look of a man carrying something he does not know how to put down.
A cup on an altar. They drink their god's blood from it. Well. It was made to hold something.
Promise to look for the cup
Tell him what you saw at Saint Martin's
Tell him it was all melted long ago
Listen, and keep off the grass
The weaver's hand
A man sits bound by the hearth of the head house, and a woman with her hand wrapped in linen sits opposite him. The household is waiting for someone who is nobody's cousin.

A long hall-house with cattle stalls at one end and a hearth at the other: a careful proud householder stands by the fire; a weaver with a bandaged hand and a furious older woman on one bench, a bound man on the other; a bolt of grey-blue cloth with one yellow thread laid on the floor between; firelight.

The law as it was said to me: who strikes the hand of a woman that weaves the fine cloth pays a quarter more than for another's hand. And who breaks a weaving hut by night answers with his life, or buys it back.
My selvedge has a yellow thread in it. I would know it across a field. He says he bought the bolt honestly on the Almere shore. Then somebody there sold it to him with my woman's blood on the door.
You are nobody's cousin here. An oath from a man with no kin on either side weighs double. Will you swear to what you saw of that bolt, if you saw it?
You swore, and it held. The terp does not forget a stranger's oath. We have so few.
Swear to what you saw: the yellow thread, and who carried the bolt
Speak for his life, and put twenty pennies toward the ransom
Say you saw nothing you could swear to
Sicco of the flats
At low water a man is walking the flats with a fish spear and a basket, a mile from anything. He sees your boat lying on the mud and comes over, talking before he is in earshot.

Vast grey tidal flats at low water under a pale sky: a cheerful barefoot fisherman with a fish spear and a basket on his back wades a shallow gully toward a small boat lying on the mud; withies marking a channel; the terp a dark bump on the horizon.
The Vlie is a road with no edges. I know where the edges are today. Ask me again tomorrow.
Old Gerlef at the Maas mouth says a pilot tells the truth about water and lies about everything else. I met him once, at Dorestat. We talked a whole night.
You have Gerlef's marks? From his own mouth? Sit down. Say them. No, do not: he would know.
A season in your boat, and I have a name at Dorestat. My brother-in-law has only a bigger boat.
There is a girl at the weaving huts. Her mother has not noticed. Her mother notices a dropped thread at forty paces.
Take him aboard as pilot for the season (10 d in hand)
Pay him to walk you over the Vlie marks at low water (15 d)
Let him talk
Twelve pennies in a knot
A small quick woman has the crew sitting and eating before any of you has said who you are. She watches one of them eat more closely than the others.

The hearth end of a Frisian long house, cattle stalls in shadow beyond: a small upright old widow ladles from a pot for four boatmen; one, a steady weathered steersman, eats without looking up; a knotted linen cloth lies on a shelf by the salt box; warm firelight.
Eat first. Names after. Does my son keep the fasts?
She asks that every time. I keep them. Tell her.
That cloth with the knot in it? It is nothing. It is twelve pennies. It is not for spending.
So the widow at Dorestat told you. Then you know what the knot is: his ship's boy's wage from that voyage, twenty years unspent. Let it be the first silver of the price.
It is paid? Say it again. Say it slowly.
Take the knotted cloth, to be laid down first at York
Tell her he keeps every fast, and two she has not heard of
Eat, thank her, and ask nothing
Boniface's month
The marsh is full for once: boats on the creek, people on every path to the mound. It is the martyr's month, and the church will not hold them.

A wooden church on a raised mound in open salt marsh, a crowd of plain marsh people spilling down the slope; a practical farmer-like priest stands at the church door with a book; a tall man in a travelling cloak holds a horse at the edge of the crowd; bright June sky, larks.
This is Boniface's month. On this ground they killed him and those who were with him, in my father's time. All month they come, and I read the names. It takes as long as it takes.
Liudger preaches from the church door, in Frisian, because the church will not hold them. Afterwards he will ask you what the sea is saying. Have an answer.
The altar wants wax and the Mass wants wine. This marsh gives neither. Every year a boat brings them, or does not.
Your wax burned from the Gospel to the last blessing. I said the name of your house. The marsh heard it.
Give a cake of wax for the altar
Sell the church a cask of wine at a fair price (56 d)
Stand through the Mass with the crew
The Aalsum cloth
At Aalsum the weaving house is half sunk in the mound, cool and dim, with four looms going. The woman who owns them puts a fold of cloth into your hand without a word.

A sunken-floored weaving hut with upright looms and rows of clay loom weights: a proud careful weaver holds out a fold of fine grey-blue twill; behind her two girls at the looms; light falling down the entrance steps.
Feel it. No: with the back of the hand. Thiadbod's man felt it with his fingers and offered half. I have not forgotten the offer or the fingers.
I do not want a buyer. I want the same buyer, every year at shearing, so that I need not sell to whoever lands.
You said you would come back at shearing. The bolts are put by, with a stick through the fold so that nobody sells them by mistake.
Shearing is done, and here you are. Then it is true what the widow at Dorestat says of your house.
Buy two bolts at her price (88 d)
Buy two bolts, and promise to come each year at shearing (88 d)
Take the two bolts she has put by (80 d)
Feel the cloth with the back of the hand, and say it is good
The priest in the sheep-house
Tetta carries a bowl out across the marsh after dark, and comes back without it. When she sees that you saw, she takes you out to the sheep-house herself.

A turf sheep-house on open marsh at dusk: a thin young man in a shepherd's cloak, a wrapped book held against his chest, crouches among ewes behind a hurdle; a lean woman in a blue gown stands in the low doorway holding a rushlight shielded by her hand; far off, the mound and one small boat.
I set out one bowl more than there are people at my fire. You counted. Most men do not count bowls.
Unno's men look into boats at the river mouth while his word runs. They look for Franks, and for books. A book can go under sailcloth. So can a thin man.
I was not in the chapel when they burned it. I have asked myself since whether I should have been. I can pay nothing. I want passage to Traiectum.
Your cloak is warm. I cough less. The ewes have not noticed the difference.
Take him aboard under the sailcloth
Leave him a cloak and bread, and say nothing
Tell Tetta you count nothing
The bowl of water
An old man and his wife are waiting at the crossing with a wooden bowl and a skin of sweet water. The ferryman is asleep in the bottom of his own boat.

A muddy river crossing at the mouth of a wide estuary: a courteous white-haired old man with a wooden bowl and his small wife with a water skin stand by a drawn-up ferry in which a man lies asleep; far over the water low marsh and a few sheep-houses; a fresh wind, running cloud.
The ferryman is drunk, and a child is dying at the sheep-houses over the water. No priest dares the road. I have a bowl and a skin of sweet water, and I was told what to say.
You rowed me, tide by tide. I owe you a story. I pay a part each night and stop where it is best; that is how a debt is kept alive.
Liudger is back, and teaching me psalms. I knew the wars of the old kings by heart before I knew one of them. There is room in a head for both, if nobody tidies it.
I was blind three years. Then I was not. Do not ask me how. I was told to say nothing while he lives, and he lives.
Row him over to the sheep-houses and back
Sit by Tetta's fire and hear the part he owes you
Give him a penny for the ferryman
Wish him a dry crossing
The rain pond
By the rain pond at the foot of the mound a very old woman is sorting leaves on a cloth. She does not look up, but she moves the cloth so that your shadow is off it.

A round clay-lined pond at the foot of a grassy mound: a very old upright woman in an undyed gown sorts herbs on a cloth, knotted cords and small pots beside her; sheep drinking at the far side; still grey light, the pond reflecting sky.
Baptised twice, by order. It ran off both times. Sit down, you are standing in my light.
The old gods have come home, they are saying on the mound. Then they will find the place much as they left it, and one frightened boy hiding among the ewes.
For sores that will not close there is a salve. I do not sell it for coin. Who is it for, and how long has she had it?
It will ease and not mend. I said so. Did you say so when you gave it?
How is the steersman's knee? I knew his mother on the islands.
Give a bundle of fleeces for the salve, and promise to say it will not mend
Let her look at the crew's hands and coughs (a wheel of cheese)
Tell her the knee is as it was
The night hull
The ferryman of the Nesse is waiting on the creek bank when you come in, looking at the water and not at you. He counts your waterline with his eyes.

A muddy creek mouth under a low mound in the last of the moonlight: a broad short ferryman with a sounding pole twice his height stands on the bank; a small boat riding deep below him; further up the creek the dark shape of a larger clinker hull with no light; mist on the water.
Twelve, an arm long. Eilbern's knots. Bring her into the creek and wait till the moon is down; there is a hull lying there, bound north.
They are for a man called Asulf at Sliesthorp. He pays for blades in silver by weight, or in people. I take the silver.
The watch at the river mouth tonight is two old men and a boy. I would not say so if it were otherwise.
Since the emperor's law it is a man's goods, and worse, to carry these east. So the price is better.
Hand the bundles over at moonset
Take them to the watch at the river mouth
Sink them in the creek, and tell him the toll man took them
The bell on the oak branch
A tall man leading a horse comes down from the mound to meet the boat. Beside the black posts of the old church a plank roof is going up, and a small bell hangs from an oak branch.

A grassy mound with the charred posts of a burned church and a new plank roof half raised beside them: a tall gentle priest in a travelling cloak holds a horse's bridle with one hand and steadies a pale young priest climbing out of a boat with the other; a small bell on an oak bough; clear morning.
You carried my priest, and he is green but whole. He tells me he looked at the water the whole way, against advice.
Nobody is punished who comes to be shriven. I say it on every mound. Some believe it sooner than others.
The bell hangs from an oak branch until there is a roof. Ring it once. You carried it; you should know what you carried.
This is twice that your boat has moved a priest for me. I keep few lists. You are on one.
Ring the bell once
Ask him for a word to the bishop for your house
Ask only where the cloth is cheapest
Bread for cloth
Word that a boat has grain aboard is round the mound before your rope is fast. A woman comes down to the landing alone, and the others stop what they are doing to listen.

A terp landing in a hungry year: a gaunt straight-backed farm woman stands at the water's edge facing a small boat with sacks under its deck boards; behind her other women at a well have stopped with their buckets half raised; a priest with a wooden measure on the path; thin cattle, pale sky.
Have you rye under your boards? Say it straight.
Nobody on the row has coin. A cloak for a sack, then two cloaks. Do not make me say three.
The head of the house will not beg. So I am asking, which is a different thing.
No grain boat since Easter. Butter is cheap, because there is nothing to put it on.
A sack buys a bolt of blue on this mound, and nobody haggles. We heard the king has named a price. We have not heard what it is.
The bishop writes that grain goes by the king's measure and at the king's price: rye three pennies. Let me hold the measure, and I will write to Traiectum who sold fair.
There is the silver that was to go with my daughter. I had rather you took cheese and hides.
Sell four sacks of rye at a fair count, paid in cheese and hides
Take the dowry silver: forty pennies for four sacks
Give a sack at the church door, or where a church should be
Say the grain is spoken for
No grain boat has reached the Frisian terps since Easter. Rye is dear at Doccinga and Winaldum, and it is paid for in cloth, cheese and hides.
A cask of Rhine wine that fetches fifty pennies on the dams at Dorestat fetches eighty on the Strand at Lundenwic, when a Frisian can land there.
On the Almere a cargo that pays the king's tenth by day sometimes changes boats by night, at the eel stakes below Medemelacha.
The king's toll
The toll man comes down to the boat with his tally stick. The king's tenth is taken on what you sell here, and he asks what you carry.
A new hull. The king's tenth is taken on what you sell here, when you sell it. What I look for now is what may not leave the realm at all. Name what is in her.
The same hull. Name what is in her, as you did before.
You hid nothing last time. I looked.
That was a kind thought, last time. I have forgotten it, as a man in my place must.
Last time you showed me a skin with a seal on it. It was good. I had it read to me twice, in case it was not.
Last time there was more under your ballast than ballast. I tap everything of yours now. Stand back from the boards.
You know the law. No mail coat leaves the realm, and no Christian is sold out of it. I say it to every hull, so that none can say he was not told.

The emperor's law since Thionville: no swords and no mail to the east or the north, but through the king's posts. What is found is forfeit, half to the palace and half to the man who finds it. I am the man who finds it.
She sits deep. Name what is in her, from the stern forward.
Empty. Then there is nothing to toll until you sell, and nothing to talk about either.
Declare the cargo
Hide the swords under the ballast
Give him something (12 d)
Show the charter
The bench inside the gate
Inside the gate a man sits on the porter's bench with his back to the grey stone, and does not look out at the strand. Hadda the prior has the begging bowl on his knee and is counting it.

A Roman gateway of grey tuff with an oak door standing open: in its cold shadow a young boatman sits on a bench, hands between his knees, beside an old prior counting a wooden bowl; beyond the arch a bright strand with boats drawn up.
He came in at this gate before the last feast with another man's blood on his sleeve. Inside the arch nobody may lay a hand on him. Outside it he is worth what his kin can pay.
A boat pole, on the strand at Dorestad, over a berth. I meant his shoulder. His brothers will take silver and have named it. I am twenty pennies short, and I cannot go out to earn them.
The church feeds him and the law waits for him. I have fed him eleven weeks. He eats like a man with a clear conscience.
Your man went out at the gate with the price paid and his hands open. He poles for the Vecht men now. Give him a season.
He left this with me for you. I counted it, and then again, because it was more than you lent. I have taken nothing for the keeping. I mention it.
The bench is empty. It will not stay so. Men have tempers and boats have poles.
The bowl is for those along the wall. It does not ask who they struck.
Lend him the twenty pennies
Take what he left with the prior
Put two pennies in the bowl
Wish them both a good day and go in
A pilgrim on the mud
At the ebb the ships sit upright on the grey mud. Beside the English one a man in a travelling cloak stands with a staff and a satchel, looking at each hull in turn as if one of them might be Rome.

Low tide in a creek behind dunes: ships upright on shining mud, a tall-stemmed English hull among broad Frisian ones; a pilgrim with staff and satchel stands in the mud to his ankles, and an English skipper leans on his rail above him. Wide pale sky, gulls.
God keep you. I am for Rome, for the apostles' graves. This ship goes no further. They say the road begins at Dorestad, up the river. Are you for the river?
Up there the king's man takes a tenth and looks in every sack. Here I sell on the mud and go home on the first east wind. The holy man can walk, or find a Frisian.
I can pay eight pennies. The rest is for the mountains. They tell me there are men in the mountains who also take a tenth.
I can pay eight pennies, or I can say your name at Saint Peter's. I am told merchants prefer the pennies. I do not judge.
You took the last one up the river. Good. They pray all the way over, and the crew begin to think they know something.
Give him passage to Dorestad for his eight pennies
Carry him for nothing, and ask to be named at Rome
Tell him you are bound down the coast
What stood at the west end
By the grey cross at the west end a monk sits on his heels in the marram grass with a wax tablet on his knee and nothing written on it. The sheep keep their distance. So does everyone else.

A bare grassy place at the end of a street of oak houses: a weathered plain oak cross taller than a man, mussel shells at its foot; a young monk crouches beside it with an empty wax tablet, looking up at the merchant. Sheep grazing well back; wind in the dune grass, grey light.
My abbot has asked a great teacher to write the saint's life. The teacher asks what is still said where it happened. I have been here four days. They sell me cheese and tell me the weather.
You they talk to. Will you ask the old people what stood here, and who struck the bishop, and what became of him? I will write no name you tell me not to write.
My grandmother saw it. The idol down, the sword on the bishop's head, and no blood. She said the keeper was dead on the third day. She also said the sword was blunt.
In my house he died of a fever and of shame, and the bishop's men wanted him dead sooner and were stopped. I am his son's son's son. Do not give that man my name.
Give him both tellings, and no name
Take him to Bernhild's door, and say the brooch-maker's forefather held the sword
Tell him that nobody here remembers anything
A coffin of boat planks
Bernhild is waiting at the head of the creek, which she has never done. Her sister died in the night. The menders have a hollowed trunk and no lid for it, and she has come to ask you for something.

A long grave field fenced with oak pales between low houses and a dune, its gate two great tree trunks: a hollowed-trunk coffin on trestles without a lid, a broad plain woman in a dark shawl standing by it with her hands folded, a sheepdog at her heel; low mounds in rows behind, a grey still morning.
Thiadwih is dead. We bury our own in boat wood here, wood that has been somewhere. I want the lid to come from a boat that carried something for her. Yours did.
She will have a penny on her right shoulder like anyone. Nobody saw her face in eleven years. They will not see it now either. I have closed it.
She has asked nobody for anything since the day I met her. Mind how you answer. The whole street will know what you said before the tide turns.
Lift the bottom boards out of your own boat for the lid
Buy good old planks from the menders for her (10 d)
Take a corner of the coffin, and stand through the burying
The menders' bank
At the head of the creek a barge lies on rollers with three strakes off her. A man splits an oak log with wedges, slowly, as if it were the last oak log in the world. On this island it nearly is.

A firm bank at the head of a tidal creek: a flat barge on rollers with planks missing, old planks stacked by length under a hide, a mender driving wedges into an oak log, a tar pot smoking; behind, a tall-stemmed English ship propped upright. Afternoon, a west wind.
We have sheep, salt and sand. Every plank on this bank came here as a ship. If you have oak in her, say so before you say good day.

The English lads on that tall one have a saying. A thing with one foot and a great many ribs, a mouth in its middle, that goes over the plain and brings men their food. They would not tell me. They laughed.
You have it. I can see you have it. Say it, and I will give you their words for it, as near as a Frisian ear could hold them.
Your oak is in that barge now, third strake. She will float it to Dorestad and back before you are home.
Sell him two loads of oak at the island's price (42 d the load)
Take the English saying away to think on
Tell him what has one foot and many ribs
Watch him split the log, and learn something
The watcher on the dune

From the top of the high dune you can see the whole street, the marsh behind it, and white water on the shoals to the north-west. A boy lies in the grass on his belly, chewing a stalk, watching the sea and you by turns.

The crest of a tall grassy dune: a boy of ten lying on his belly in marram grass, chin on his fists, looking out to sea; below on one side a long street of thatched oak houses and a marsh with sheep, on the other grey sea breaking white on shoals. Big sky, clouds building in the west.
Bernhild's ewes lay facing the land this morning. All of them. Nobody here sails tomorrow. You can, you are not from here.
I am paid in bread to see sails. Two since dawn, both ours. If I see a striped one I am to run and not shout. I have never seen a striped one.
The salt men light the hearths after Lammas. Before that there is no salt here worth your sack. After Martinmas the river boats have had it all.
You sailed. I watched you past the shoal. Then I could not see you for the rain. The ewes were right.
Lie another day in the creek, as the sheep say
Sail on the morning ebb all the same
Give the boy a penny to watch your boat with the rest (1 d)
The tan pits

At the marsh edge the square pits lie full of brown water, hides sunk under hurdles. A man with arms stained to the elbow hauls one out, looks at it, and puts it back for another month. The smell arrived before you did.

Square pits of dark brown water at the edge of a marsh, hides weighted under wattle hurdles; a heap of ox horns, strips of leather on a rail; a man with tan-stained forearms lifting a dripping hide on a pole. Flat light, sheep far off, the houses upwind.
Green hides, five to the bundle, twelve pennies. Up the river they will ask you fifteen and tell you about the journey. I never went anywhere. That is the three pennies.
Here is one my father had off an Englishman. Alive I break the ground. Dead I bind the strong and the weak, and a man drinks from my belly. He never told me the answer. He said I was standing in it.
You are smiling. You know what I am standing in.
They built the street upwind of me. Then they come down here for shoes.
Buy two bundles of hides at the pit (24 d)
Take his father's riddle away with you
Tell him what he is standing in
Breathe through your mouth and walk on
Six pennies the measure

The king is on the hill and the bank is thick with people who have nothing to sell. A clerk stands on a cart tail with a sheet of skin, and reads the king's new law to them in a loud flat voice, twice.

A crowded river bank under a high wall of grey Roman tuff in a cold spring: a thin clerk standing on a cart tail reading from a parchment, thin people in the crowd looking up, a heavy cellarer with keys at his belt watching the merchant's boat; sacks under a hide, bare willows, a raw wind.
By the measure: oats two pennies, barley three, rye four, cleaned wheat six. Who buys at harvest for two to sell at four or six, that we call shameful gain. So says the king.
Who buys from need, to keep for himself or to share with others, that we call trade. I am told to read that part slowly.

You sit low in the water for a man with nothing to sell. I will take it by the king's measure at the king's price, and pay on the nail. It is less than the bank will give you by dusk. It is also the law.
Your measure was full last time. The clerk wrote down who sold. On this hill that is worth more than the pennies.
Sell the cellar four sacks of rye at the lawful four
Keep the hold shut for a dearer day up the river
Hear the law out to the end, and learn the prices
The masons' tally

Wendilgard's is full of stone dust and big hands. The king's masons sit along one wall, each with a notched stick in front of him where another man would have a purse. She ladles, and cuts a notch, and ladles.

A low smoky ale-house of posts and wattle with a hearth in the middle: a row of masons grey with stone dust on a bench, each with a tally stick before him; a broad laughing woman ladling ale from a tub with a knife in her other hand. Firelight, wet leg bindings steaming.
A king's house, and it stands on my ale. They were not paid at Martinmas. They drink on a stick, and I burn the sticks when the silver comes. I have a fine pile of sticks.
Bring me barley. Six sacks before the next court and I will pay over the price, because a court drinks a month's brewing in a week and pays in thanks.
A man from Dorestad was asking after you. Big ship, soft voice, gave my girls a comb each. He wanted to know what you owe and to whom. I said you paid me. It is all I know and all he got.
Hostages? I poured for the men who brought them over, the year the dukes bowed. Boys, roped in fours. The tally went up the hill. Engilbald has every skin they ever wrote, and he likes to be asked.
You said six sacks. I told the masons there would be ale at Easter. Do not make a liar of me in front of masons.
Take her order: six sacks of barley
Pay off the masons' sticks for the evening (6 d)
Ask her where the tally of the hostages went
Sit where she tells you, and listen
The Batua crossing

A broad punt lies grounded where the cart track comes down to the water. Across the brown river the far bank is a low green line with cattle on it. The ferryman sits mending a net, and watches the current and not you.

A flat ferry punt grounded on a muddy river bank beside a cart track, a net drying on stakes; a weathered ferryman sitting cross-legged with a netting needle, eyes on the brown water; far across, a low green shore of willows with cattle. Still, overcast, a heron on a stake.
She has a bar on the north side this year that was not there at Easter. Keep to the outside of the bend going down. I tell everyone once.
Over there they make more cheese than they can eat and nobody climbs the hill to sell it. A penny over, a penny back, and the cheese is half what the bank asks.
Three boats came down in the night without a light. Laden. Nobody up there asked. I do not ask either. I only count.
The clerk's house that is never quiet? I live on its roof. The house is loud, the guest is dumb, and both go the same way. I took his supper out of it this morning.
You haul like a man who has hauled before. Sit. I will tell you where she shoals below the wall. It is worth more than the fare.
Cross with him and buy at the farms (9 d)
Help him haul and mend the net
Tell him the clerk up there has a question for him
The toll at the river mouth

The emperor keeps Easter on the hill. Under the old wall the Tiel men are putting on their good cloaks, and Sibrand is counting heads. He counts yours, and looks pleased, and then looks at you to see whether he should be.

Easter morning under a high Roman wall of grey tuff with jackdaws: a knot of river merchants in their best cloaks, one quick dry man at the front beckoning the merchant to join them; a royal chamberlain with a staff waiting at the foot of the path up to a mended stone hall. Bright cold sun, banners above.

Dirk has a fort at the mouth and takes toll of every keel for England. We pay the king at Tiel. Now we pay twice. Today we say it to the emperor's face. Come and stand with us. It costs nothing but Dirk.
They know our faces up there, and they are tired of them. A house from another bank, saying what he took from it last season, in pennies: that they would hear.
One of you speaks, and briefly. The emperor has heard the bishop already and has a Mass to hear after you. Who speaks?
You spoke well. They are sending an army down by water. I am told it will be over by Lammas. I have been told things before.
The count's steward knows what was said in that hall. He knew it by Whitsun. We have been wondering who writes so quickly.
Speak for them before the emperor: what the count took, in pennies
Stand among them in your good cloak, and say nothing
Hold your tongue in the hall, and send the count word of what was said
The captive in the king's house

A fence of sharpened timber runs round the hilltop and long ships lie under it where the landing was. The man at the gap in the fence looks into your boat, weighs a sack in his hand, and waves you in. Inside, by a fire, a young man in a good cloak is watching you.

Winter on a hilltop: a fresh earth bank and sharpened palisade, long ships with shields drawn up below, snow, many fires; inside the gap a fair-haired young captive in a fine dirty cloak sitting by a fire, a Northman with an axe leaning beside him; far off across white fields the tents of an army.
