Grain, ale, meat. We weigh silver for it and we weigh it true. The king out there pays in promises. Who would you rather feed?
You trade with them. I do not blame you, it is winter. I am Eberhard, Meginhard's son. My mother's steward waits at Daventre. Will you carry a message out with your empty sacks?
They count silver by weight and they count it well. She must not send light coin. Tell her that before you tell her I am alive.
You have not been to Daventre. I can see it in how you stand. The frost will not last for ever, and when the river opens they go north and I go with them.
You came back through the fence. Then she has an answer. Say it quickly. They are watching.
Carry his word out to Daventre
Give him his mother's answer
Sell the Northmen four sacks of rye, by weight of silver
Keep to the bank below, and to your own business
Evesa's man
A grey man in a lord's livery has stood on the bank since the frost came, asking every boat from the Waal the same question. He asks it of you before your painter is fast.

A frozen river bank with boats drawn up and ice along the edge: a grey-haired steward in a good fur-lined cloak with a sealed bag at his belt, standing very straight at the water's edge, breath smoking, as a small boat noses in. A wooden church on a dune behind, snow on the thatch.
You are from the Waal. Is the count's son alive? Say that first. Then say what they ask for him, and then I will remember my manners.
My lady has the silver. She has had it since the first frost. What she has not had is a man who has stood inside that fence and come out again.
Tell him the young man lives, and what is asked
Tell him, and warn him: they weigh every coin, send nothing light
Tell him you must see to your boat first
Pegs and strings

Along the sand ridge pegs and strings mark out ground where no house stands yet. A sour-faced man is walking one of the strings with a measuring cord, counting under his breath. When he sees your boat he stops counting.

A sand ridge above a river with a single row of timber houses and, between them, plots marked with pegs and taut strings; a lean sour man in a Frisian cloak holding a knotted measuring cord, a spade stuck in a heap of cut sods beside him. Clear windy day, the wooden church beyond.

You had a jetty at Dorestad, or your father had. Then you had better have this before the bishop's steward sells it to a man from nowhere. Three hundred pennies. The ground must be raised with sods. It always must.
Eighteen paces on the ridge and a boat path to the bank. At Dorestad I would have called it a dog's yard. Here it is a street.
I have told the steward the string is spoken for. He does not believe me, but he believes my temper. Two hundred and sixty, to a man who has carried my sods.
They wintered in the king's house at Noviomagus. From there to here is three days, for men who row for pleasure. Buy, and keep your goods where you can carry them.
Buy the plot beside his (300 d)
Buy the plot at the price he holds it for (260 d)
Carry sods on his plot for a day, and ask him to hold the string
Walk the string with him, and promise nothing
Who crossed
The ferry barge lies nosed into the bank beside the post with the horn on it. The ferryman is cutting a notch in a long stick already crowded with notches. He finishes the notch before he looks up.

A flat ferry barge with a pole and two oars against a sandy river bank, a post with a horn hanging from it; an old Saxon ferryman seated on the gunwale notching a long tally stick with a knife; across the brown river low empty grass and a cart track. Morning mist lifting.
A penny for a man, two for a horse, nothing for news if you bring some. Forty carts for the host since Easter. Somebody on the Weser will sleep badly.
I do not see who crosses at night. I am old and I sleep. Remember that I said so, if anyone asks you.
The ale-wife's boy. Yes. I have carried many boys. Ask me again when I know which way your boat points.

I never told her all of it. I carried them west, roped in fours. On the far bank the palace's men from Noviomagus took the rope and a tally. The tally named the lord each boy was for. Look for the tally.
A hand lower than when you left. Keep to the east bank past the brook. And if you find that tally, read it to her slowly.
Pay your penny, and give him the river's news (1 d)
Ask him where the hostages were handed over
Tell the count's men what the ferryman does not see at night
Nod to him, and ask nothing
Across one cloth

Mass is over and the churchyard has turned into a market without anybody deciding it should. On a cloth between two grave posts stand six crocks tied down with bladder. The woman behind them names her price in Saxon, and a Frankish soldier answers in Frankish, slowly, as if to a horse.

Trodden ground between a wooden church and a row of houses, graves marked with posts: goods laid out on cloths and cart tails, a Saxon woman kneeling behind crocks of honey, a Frankish soldier bending to bargain, a priest in the church door watching; eels in baskets, a horse on a halter. Bright noon after Mass.
Twenty the crock. Heath honey, this summer's. He offers me twelve and says it louder each time. I heard him the first time.
You have a man aboard who speaks like a person. For him, sixteen. Tell him the bees are baptised. It is what they want to hear.
Saxons on the north side, Franks on the south, and neither will take the peace from the other. But they will sell each other a horse before they are out of the yard. I call that a beginning.
You want to know what a grown man says at the font, east of here? I have it by heart. I have said it for men with a spear behind them and for men with none. The words are the same. The men are not.
Buy two crocks of heath honey at her price (40 d)
Let your Saxon speaker buy the two crocks (32 d)
Ask the priest for the words of the vow
Walk the cloths, and buy nothing
Rodulf is dead

You have rowed south with one thing aboard that nobody on this river has yet. The bishop's clerks sit in the doorway of his house for the light. On the bank Thiadlef is already walking towards your boat, because you came in too fast for a man with nothing to tell.

A fenced timber hall near a wooden church, clerks with wax tablets sitting in its doorway under a swallow's nest; a small boat just grounded on the bank, its crew still at the oars; a sour lean merchant striding down from the houses towards it. Midsummer light, long evening.
You came up that last reach as if the bank were on fire. What is it? I will pay to hear it before the bishop does. I paid Rodulf three summers running; I have a right to bad news about him.
The bishop is at his prayers. If you have something from the north, say it to me and I will judge whether it is worth breaking them for.
Tell it at the bishop's door first: Rodulf dead, his men sworn out of the kingdom
Sell it on the bank first, to every man who ever paid Rodulf
Say only that the wind was fair, and keep it another day
Mass at the turn of the tide

The whole strand is walking up to the cross on the ridge. A boat has come over from the far shore with a priest in the bow, holding a wrapped book against his chest to keep the spray off it. There is no bell. Somebody beats a cauldron.

A plain wooden cross on a low marsh ridge above a tidal creek, a few dozen people in their feast-day cloaks gathering round it, a hoarse priest stepping out of a small boat with a wrapped book held to his chest; a woman beating an iron cauldron with a ladle. Slack water, gulls, high thin cloud.
God keep you. You are in time: Mass at the cross when the tide turns. The tide is the only bell I have, and it keeps better hours than most.
A roof over the cross and a bell to call the strand, so that I need not shout against the wind. I have asked the abbot. The abbot has asked the saint. The saint is thinking.
The merchant who stood through the whole Mass. There were four of you. I remember all four, and I have told the abbot's man which boats they were.
You asked me about the path. I have thought about why I was angry. It is because they walk it in their good shoes.
Stand through the whole Mass with the crew
Give toward a roof for the cross, and a bell (6 d)
Ask him where the path behind his own church goes
The racks and the salt fires

Down the strand split fish hang in rows on poles, stiff as shingles, and beyond them grey smoke lies flat over the marsh where the salt burners are at work. The wind decides which of the two you smell first.

A flat marsh shore: rows of split fish drying on pole racks, a fisherman turning them; beyond, low turf-built hearths with flat pans, a man raking grey ash, heaps of cut peat, smoke lying level in the wind. Summer haze, a hull on the mud behind.
It is grey because it was peat before it was salt. Burn the peat, wash the ash, boil the wash. It salts a herring as well as the white, and the herring has never complained.
Two pennies the sack here. At Dorestad they will show you the same sack for three and tell you it came from the western sea.
Four pennies the bundle, twenty to the bundle. They keep a year if you keep them dry. So do I.
Back for more? Then somebody up the river ate it and lived. I will tell my wife. She worries.
Buy four sacks of grey salt at the fires (8 d)
Buy three bundles of dried fish off the racks (12 d)
Taste a grain and a flake, and walk back up the strand
The notched stick

The bank you knew is torn out for half its length, and a boat lies in the nettles behind the row where the water left it. A woman has walked in from the lake hamlet to meet you. She has a hazel stick in her hand, split down its length, and no purse.

A broken timber-faced bank on a peat-brown stream, a stranded boat lying in nettles behind a row of thatched houses with a tide line of mud across their walls; a lean weathered woman of forty holding out a split hazel tally stick in both hands. Grey sky to every edge, dead reeds.
Eleven drowned on the lake. Nine beasts in ten gone. The seed rye spoiled and the wells salt. I have counted it all and it comes to nothing I can pay you with.
So. A notch for each sack. You keep one half and I keep the other. When there are calves again I pay, and a third over. My word is the only thing the water did not get into.
And if you have nothing to sell, leave me a cask that will hold sweet water. We are drinking rain off the thatch.
There are calves on the dry strip. Bring out your half. There. They fit. I never doubted mine; I am glad to see yours.
Give her four sacks of rye on the stick
Lay your half of the stick beside hers
Sell her two sacks for what silver the hamlet can find (10 d)
Leave her an empty cask for sweet water, and your good wishes
The bead bench

In a lean-to against the wind a man sits over a small clay hearth, turning an iron rod in the flame with a bead of blue glass growing on its end. On the bench by his elbow, among the rods, lies half a silver coin.

A lean-to on a terp with a small clay hearth and bellows: a bead maker turning an iron rod with a glowing blue bead on its tip, strings of yellow and blue beads hanging from a nail, broken green glass in a basket; on the bench a cut half of a silver coin with flowing script. Close warm light, wind outside.
Every bead on that nail was a Frank's drinking cup. They break them, the river brings them, I melt them. If you have broken glass in her, I pay better than the midden.
That? A Dane gave it me for combs, at their market. Half a coin, cut clean, with writing no priest here can read. He put it on a scale. He did not count it. He weighed it.

I have been thinking about your question. Up there a whole coin and a broken ring are the same thing if they weigh the same. A man could carry his scraps north and be rich. Or be robbed. One of the two.
Buy two strings of his beads (20 d)
Sell him a load of raw glass (30 d)
Ask him about the cut coin, and how the Danes reckon
The spring on the mound

Half way up the mound sweet water comes out of the clay into a stone-lined hollow, in a country where every other well tastes of the sea. A very old woman sits beside it on a three-legged stool, as she has, they say, most days since before you were born.

A stone-lined spring in the flank of a grassy mound with a wooden church on top: a very old woman in a dark hood on a three-legged stool beside the water, one hand raised flat above her own head to show how a book was held; a crewman filling a small cask. Salt marsh to the horizon, larks, a mild day.
I saw it. I was a child, carrying water. He put the book over his head, so, with both hands. The sword came down on the book. I have told it sixty years and never changed a word.
When they raised the mound for his church they dug for clay and found this. Sweet. In this marsh. Drink, and then tell me it is only water.
The island priest filled his flask here and said that where he was born the holy water was drawn in silence. He did not say which he liked better. I told him here we talk.
You asked how old I was. Old enough to carry two pails and young enough to run. I did not run. That is how I saw it.
Drink, and hear her out to the end
Fill the boat's casks, and leave a penny on the stone (1 d)
Ask her how old she was that morning
To none but King Louis

There are more men on the long mound than live in the whole district, and none of them is talking. Rodulf the Dane is dead, with hundreds of his people. The rest are shut in a building, and an old Northman who farms here is telling the Frisians what to do with them.

A crowded terp in June: armed Frisian farmers standing silent round a barred timber building, a heap of silver arm-rings, coins and cups on a cloak on the ground, a calm white-haired old Northman in a plain farm tunic pointing at it with an open hand; a priest and a count's man beside him. Long light, smoke from somewhere behind.

Do not kill them. Dead men's kin come back. Take what they carry, and hostages, and their oath never to enter King Louis's kingdom again. I know what such an oath is worth to them. It is worth this once.
Yours is the only keel in the creek that is not theirs. The bishop and the count's friends in the south will pay for this word. Every merchant who ever paid Rodulf will pay more.
Or stay, and bring your scale. There is more silver on that cloak than the mounds can count, and nobody here trusts his neighbour's weights today. A tenth for the weighing, before the priest.
You have a merchant's face. You are reckoning. Good. Reckon this too: they asked us for tribute, and we said, to none but King Louis and his sons. Then it was said with iron. Say it so in the south.
Row south with the word before anyone else
Stay, and weigh the treasure on your scale for a tenth
Stand witness while the survivors swear, and take nothing
The ring on the sand

At low water the free men of the mound stand in a ring on the wet sand, on ground that will be sea again by evening. There is no priest among them this year and no count's man. An old man with a staff turns to your boat and the ring opens on that side.

Low tide at a river mouth: forty armed farmers standing in a ring on shining wet sand, a staff set upright in the middle, an old man with a long grey moustache pointing it towards a small boat aground at the ring's edge; behind, a terp with thatched roofs and the black posts of a burned church. Flat grey light, the sea a line far out.
A Dorestad boat. The count at Dorestad is the king's man. The king's men lie dead on the Weser this summer, and we pay no tithe and feed no priest. So I ask it in the ring, once: whose man are you?
We stand here because the sand is nobody's. Twice a day the sea takes back what was said on it. Only what is sworn stays.
You answered well in the ring last time. Men here still say it over. Lie where you lay before.
Last time your tongue cost you twelve pennies. The poor of the mound ate them. Have you a shorter answer today?
Say you are the count's debtor and nobody's man: you owe him silver as they owe him tithe
Say nothing, and set a cask of ale down inside the ring
Say you are a man with a tide to catch, and push off
At the Danes' markets silver goes by weight and not by count: a cut coin, a broken arm-ring and a king's penny are one thing on the scale.
The painted leaf

On the dams a Frisian back from Ripa has beads, combs and amber laid out on a hide. Among them lies one leaf of calfskin with red and blue letters on it. The priest of the upper church is standing over it, very still.

A hide spread on a timber dam with strings of beads, antler combs and one painted parchment leaf: a sunburned Frisian trader squats behind it, a thin priest bends over the leaf with his hands held back as from a fire; masts and the brown river behind, bright morning.
I had it at Ripa for a string of beads. The man said it was a pattern for weaving. My wife says no loom could do it. Six pennies, and it is yours to argue about.
It is a leaf of a psalter. English work: I have a letter from York in the same hand. This was cut out of a book with a knife.
A year since the holy island. They took the books for the gold on the boards. The leaves they sold by the handful, to men who took them for patterns.
A goldsmith on the beach at Ripa. He had the gold off the cover and the leaves in a basket. He named the crew that brought the book. I did not think to remember, till you asked.
Buy it, shipman. Not for me: I have not six pennies. The bishop's school would give its price ten times over. The brothers on the island would give more than silver.
Buy the leaf (6 d)
Ask the seller who sold it to him, and who brought the book
Leave it on the hide for the bead makers
The king's ships go overland

Two of the count's men are walking the dams with a tally stick, choosing boats and backs. The king's ships are to go into Saxony this summer by river and over dry land, on rollers, and somebody must haul them.

A row of timber dams with small boats between them: a Frankish officer with a tally stick points at the merchant's boat while a second man notches; a big Saxon mate turns his face away; far up the bank oxen and men drag a hull on rollers; grey windy day.
By the king's word: boats to carry rope and rollers up the river, and men to haul where the river stops. A month. You are fed, and your stick in the count's hall is remembered.
A small boat carries rope as well as any. I have you on my stick, or I have a man in your place. I do not go back to the hall with a gap.
They are hauling ships into my country. I will pull your oar anywhere. Not that rope.
Give the boat and a month to the hauling
Pay a porter to haul in your place (24 d)
Be gone on the night ebb before the stick reaches your dam
A Saxon who asks no questions

Aldswith puts your ale down and does not go away. At the dark end of the bench sits a big man whose long hair has been cut short, badly, with a knife. He has asked her for a berth. He has asked that nobody ask him anything.

The dark end of a smoky hall-house: a big fair man with roughly cropped hair sits alone with his hands round a cup, a bundle at his feet; a broad ale-wife leans to the merchant's ear in the foreground; firelight, a dog under the bench.
Strong, quiet, eats like two. No kin on this bank, and none he will name. I would ask him one or two things, son, before the count's men do. They were in yesterday, asking for a man his size.
I row. I haul. I drink my share and no more. Where I was at Easter is my own. Where my lord thinks I am is his.
The king gives Saxons to bishops and counts by the hundred, to keep. Some of them do not keep.
The count's men took him out by the back. He did not look at me. He looked at your place on the bench.
Give him the berth, and ask nothing
Tell him which boat leaves for the Almere tonight, and forget his face
Send word to the count's men
Which man

A crew in from the coast is drinking at Aldswith's as men drink who have been frightened for a month and are not any more. Their skipper is saying one thing over and over. By the door post Ravn has put his cup down.

A crowded smoky hall-house: a salt-stained Frisian skipper stands on a bench with his cup raised, his crew roaring round him; by the door post a grey Northman sits very still with his cup set down on the floor; the ale-wife counts on her fingers; night, firelight.
Godfred is dead. The king of the Danes. One of his own following did it, at home, with the emperor's host still on the Weser. The two hundred ships have gone back to bury him or to quarrel over him.
His brother's son has the kingdom and wants peace. They say it will be sworn on the Eider when the roads are dry.
It was sworn on the Eider in spring: twelve men of theirs and twelve of ours. I have the names of none of them. I have my boat back.
Which man? A king killed by his own man is one story. Which man is another. I knew some of them.
So the host comes home. Whoever is sitting on oats and salt pork at an army's price has a week to stop sitting.
Stand the crew a round and hear it from the beginning (4 d)
Sell four sacks of oats at the army's price, before the dams hear
Send the word on to the terps by the next boat north
Sit by the door post and say nothing
Catla's purse

A Svea woman in a travelling cloak is going from holy place to holy place with a heavy leather bag held in both arms, and three women of the bank beside her to say which of the poor are truly poor. On the dams, a bag like that is watched.

A timber church door standing open on a rise above two rivers: a sunburned woman in a northern travelling cloak holds a heavy leather bag in both arms, three older women of the bank beside her; thin people along the church wall; a few men on the dam below, watching; clear afternoon.

My mother Frideburg kept this silver for the poor, and died before a priest came back to Birka. She said: here there are few poor. At Dorstadt there are many churches and many poor. Give it there, with your own hand.
The women know the doors. They do not know the men on the dams. Will a shipman of this bank walk beside the bag?
Half is given, and we are all dead on our feet. She says we must drink something. Four pennies' worth of wine, she says, and counts them out of the bag herself.
Walk beside her through the dams till the bag is empty
Draw her four pennies' worth of wine from your own cask
Stand aside and watch the bag go by
The bag at the lodging
Evening. The last of the silver went at the church by the fork, and Catla set the empty bag down inside the door of her lodging. Now the women are standing round it, and nobody is sitting.

A long room with a hearth and benches at dusk: a leather bag stands open on the earth floor just inside the door, silver showing at its mouth; four women stand round it with their hands at their sides, one a sunburned northerner in a travelling cloak; the merchant in the doorway; firelight on their faces.
She set it down empty. I saw the bottom of it. Lift it. Go on. It is as heavy as when she landed. We have counted twice: all of it there, but the four pennies that went on wine.
Then what was given is given back, and what we drank is drunk. I am a merchant's daughter. I know only that it does not balance, and that I am glad.
The priest believed me sooner than I did. He says the Lord repaid the alms and kept back the wine. I poured that wine. It was good wine.
Promise to tell it at Birka as you saw it
Offer her passage home toward Birka (40 d)
Lift the bag once, set it down, and say nothing
A count of keels

You come up to the dam heads a day ahead of what you have to tell. Thiadlef is on his father's dam with a short sword on, which he never used to wear. He sees how you came in, and walks down to meet you.

A long timber dam head at dusk: a thick-set greying skipper in a worn blue cloak, a short sword at his belt, comes down the plank way toward a small boat whose crew are still at the oars; behind him storehouses with their doors barred; a red low sky down the river.
You rowed the last reach. Nobody rows that reach for pleasure. How many, and where?
The Witla pilot's count? Then it is a count. His grandfather never rounded a number in his life either.
I keep my silver where a spade can find it and a Dane cannot. Tonight a good many spades will be out. Yours too, if you have sense.
Cry it along the dams: the count of keels, and how far behind you they are
Tell Thiadlef alone, for a price (40 d)
Say nothing, and load for upriver while the dams sleep
A fire on the mark

On the dune mound the count from the island and the pilot of the bar are standing either side of the fire basket, not looking at each other. Below them half the strand's boats lie loaded, and the market hurdles are bare.

A turf mound at the seaward end of a marsh ridge with a tall post and an iron fire basket: a heavy Frankish count in a mail shirt on one side, a long-armed barefoot pilot with a notched sounding pole on the other; below, loaded boats on the mud and empty hurdles; a wide grey river mouth, evening.
A fire on this post when sails are seen. The island sees it, I call out my forty spears, and the palace has one more thing it cannot say it was not told.

A fire tells them where the houses are as well as it tells him. They went up at Whitsun by night and asked for no pilot. They know this mouth. I would rather they did not know which ridge we sleep on.
Twenty-six keels the first night and eleven the second. I counted them against the post, twice. If you are for Dorestad, take the count with you. They may listen to a boat that rowed.
Half this strand is carrying its stores inland by the creeks. Good. A man with nothing left to burn stands in the line better.
You took my count up the river. Did they dig, or did they laugh?
Take the pilot's count of keels up the river to Dorestad
Say the count is right: pay for peat, and let the fire be lit (6 d)
Say the pilot is right: no fire
Lend your boat for a tide to carry the weavers' stores up the creek
The guest's gift

No king's man looks into your hull. Two Danes do, without touching anything. A Danish shield hangs over the door of the king's house, and the red-bearded lord of the island is at home. Unno the salter is waiting outside with the strand's sacks, and speaks to you first.

The fenced yard of a long oak hall on an island of dunes, a round painted shield over its door: a short soot-grey salter with sacks on a sledge speaks low to the merchant; in the doorway behind, half in shadow, a broad red-bearded Dane with silver on his arms; wind, pale light.
He takes no toll. He takes a gift. You choose it, and he chooses whether it was enough. Last year: wine, and a good cloak. Never coin. Never a blade, good or bad.
A merchant. Good. I take no toll here. A guest brings what he thinks fitting. I see what he thinks.
Or it goes in with ours, in my sacks, and he never sees your face. He knows there are such merchants. He lets it be while the salt is good.
You came back, so I was not too dear. Sit. Drink. Tell me who is on the water.
The priests up the river will ask whether you sat at his table. They write the answer down.
Carry a cask of Rhine wine in to him yourself
Send your gift in with the strand's, in Unno's sacks (10 d)
Say you do not trade under a heathen lord, and sail on the ebb
Stand in the yard with Unno, and learn what is thought fitting
Sods for the ring

By the dunes a round bank of stacked sods is rising, as high as a man already and meant to be twice that. Every house on the strand has its stretch. Unno is cutting with the rest, and straightens his back when he sees a boat he knows.

A half-built round rampart of stacked sods behind grey dunes, a wet ditch at its foot: men and women cutting and carrying turf on hurdles; a short thick man grey with ash leans on a spade and looks toward the viewer; sheep, a huge sky, wind from the sea.
They came a week before Saint John's on the morning tide, and there was nowhere to drive a beast or a child. Now there will be. It is not a wall against the Danes. It is a wall against a morning.
Twenty paces a house. A boat that uses this strand is a house, the old women have decided. Cut for a day, or pay a digger. Nobody will say a word either way. They will only know.
My sister Berntrud went north in their ships that summer. If you lie at the Danes' markets, ask after a Frisian woman with a burn on her left wrist. Before winter. By spring they are sold on east.
On Saint Stephen's day the sea came almost over the dunes. So the old women were right about the wall, for the wrong reason.
Your stretch has grass on it now. The children call it the Dorestad piece.
Cut and carry sods with the crew for a day
Pay diggers for a full stretch, and a place inside for your goods (60 d)
Promise to ask after Berntrud in the north
Two lords in the hall

The king's house is full for the first time in years. King Charles from the west sits at one end with his bishops, and at the other, in a Frankish count's cloak, sits Rorik the Northman. Between them clerks are writing. A merchant of the river is of use to both, and both have noticed you.

A long stone hall with hangings: at the far end a king among bishops, at the near end a tall fair Northman in a Frankish cloak with gold arm rings, a small cross on his breast; clerks at a board between them; the merchant in the doorway with his cap in his hand; cold light from the door.

The king binds the Northman to him by treaty. That is the word we are to write. What he is bound to is keeping the others out of the river. You pay his toll? Then you are a witness to how he keeps it.
A merchant of my river. Good. Tell the king's clerk what you paid me last season, and whether any fleet came up while I was at home. Say it as it was. I can bear it.
Men swear to my peace here, before both of us. It costs what my toll man already takes, and it is worth a watchman at the river mouth. The king is looking. It is a good day to be seen.
You are already his man. Then say so. The king will know what a Frisian's oath to a Northman is worth by how you say it.
Swear to Rorik's peace before both lords
Tell the clerk plainly what you paid and what you saw
Sell two casks of Rhine wine to the two households while they talk
The Greek empress

The king's house on the hill is hung with black. The empress Theophanu, the Greek, mother of the boy king, has died in it nine days before Saint John's. Her body is to go up the Rhine to Colonia by ship, and at the landing a steward is counting hulls.

A river landing under a steep hill with a mended stone hall above, black cloths hanging from its windows: a long river ship with a draped bier amidships; a steward in a dark cloak counts boats on his fingers; nuns with a chest wait on the gravel; still grey midsummer morning, every head bare.
The lady goes to Saint Pantaleon at Colonia, as she asked. The king's ship carries her. I need hulls behind it for her women, her chests and her chapel. Towed, fed, and paid at Colonia.
Every boat on the river gives way and bares its head. You may be one that gives way, or one that follows. It is all the same to her now.
Wax. Every church between here and Colonia is to burn lights as she passes, and this bank has eaten its candles since Easter.
She came from the Greeks as a girl, with silk, and was called proud for it. She ruled for a child and kept his crown on him. I have buried worse Christians.
Join the ships behind her, and carry one of her women to Colonia (30 d)
Sell the church two cakes of wax for the lights, at the common price
Lie at the bank, bare your head, and let her pass
The barge bank

Downstream of the landing a flat barge stands half built on blocks, her bottom planks wider than a man's chest. Two wrights with adzes are arguing over a log. A boy boiling moss and tar looks up at your boat, and laughs.

A river bank with a half-built flat-bottomed barge on blocks, split oak logs stacked to season, wood chips everywhere: a grey wright with an adze squints at the merchant's small round-hulled boat; a boy stirs an iron pot of tar over a fire; the steep palace hill behind, afternoon haze.
A round boat, on this river. She will sail well and carry a cupboard. Ours carries a house and floats on a wet meadow. But you are from the salt end, where things have keels.
Oak I have. What I never have is tar. The pines are a month's haul up the Rhine, and the palace takes the first of every cargo for its roofs. Two barrels, and I pay over the bank.
The king's masons want stone carried by Easter, and the barge wants a week more than Easter. I have explained wood to them. They explained the king to me.
I have hauled on the tow rope to Colonia twice. It is a long way to walk for a look at a church. I would rather see what is at the other end of the water.
Your tar is in her seams, and she is as dry as a sermon.
Sell him two barrels of tar (24 d the barrel)
Take his order: four barrels of tar
Take the boy to the salt end
Watch them lay a bottom plank, and say nothing about keels
A daughter of King Cnut

At Pentecost the emperor's son Henry weds Gunhild, daughter of the dead King Cnut, in the king's house on the hill. The bank is thick with English and Danish hulls that came with the bride, and the court's buyers are paying what they are asked.

A crowded river bank under a hill crowned by a stone hall and a small eight-sided chapel hung with banners: tall-stemmed sea-going ships among river barges, casks rolling up the path; a court steward with a purse and a weathered English shipman watch the merchant's boat come in; bright early summer.
A king's wedding, an emperor's table, and three hundred guests who brought their own thirst. Wine, wax, anything that can be roasted. I pay today's price today. Tomorrow I shall be ashamed of it.

We brought her over the sea with her father's silver in her chests. He held England and Denmark, and the road to Rome open for men like us. He has lain at Winchester since the day after Martinmas, and nobody knows whose sea it is now.
They are to call her Kunigunde here, and crown her on the feast of the Apostles. She speaks Danish to her women and has not been heard to laugh.
Sell the court two casks of Rhine wine at the wedding price
Keep the feast on the bank: meat and ale for the crew (10 d)
Drink with the English crews, and learn how England stands
A leaf for the chest
You lay the painted leaf on the master's desk. He does not touch it. He fetches a clean cloth first, and then a boy to hold the lamp.

A sloped desk under a small glazed window: one parchment leaf with red and blue letters lying on a white cloth, a stooped schoolmaster bent close with his hands behind his back, a small boy holding a lamp in both hands; the great iron-bound chest in the shadow behind.
English. Northumbrian, by the hand. See how the red dots go round the great letter: they do that on the holy island, and nowhere on the Rhine. Where is the rest of the book?
A goldsmith's basket on a Danish beach. So it is true what Alfward wrote. They are selling the Psalms by the handful.
The bishop will give sixty pennies for it. I will add what a school has: an order. Calfskin, scraped thin, every spring, at a price we both write down.
Or carry it home to the island it was cut from. Their bishop will lay it on the altar. I should like to be the kind of man who told you to do that. I am telling you. I also have sixty pennies.
Sell the leaf to the school (60 d), and take the order for calfskin
Give the leaf to Saint Martin's, for the chest
Wrap it again: it is going home to the island
The tenth of the tenth

It is Saint Martin's month, and the store door stands open for what the north owes the saint. The keeper of the store has his tally board out before you have a line ashore. He has been told which boat.

The door of a half-sunk storehouse inside an old fort wall: an old monk with keys and a tally board counts cheeses stacked on a hide, a sealed leather bag and a pot of butter beside them; the merchant's crew carry hides up from the strand; November light, bare trees.
Medemelacha's tenth of the king's tenth: pennies in a sealed bag, eleven cheeses, four hides and a pot of butter. I count it once for the saint and once for the toll man, who will ask.
The seal is whole. His own boat brings it wet, and he swears at the Vecht the whole length of the guest table. I shall miss that.
I cut a stick for him: received, and by whose hull. Carry it north. A toll man who holds a saint's stick for you has finished looking in your boat.
Hand it over, counted twice
Hand it over a cheese short, and say the Almere was rough
The name inside the lid

Scaffolds stand on the old walls, and the bishop who brought the see home is on one of them with lime on his shoes, pointing. He comes down the ladder when he hears that a boat is in which can carry weight.

A Roman fort wall of pale tuff under timber scaffolding, masons and hoists: a tall fair bishop in a fur-edged cloak climbs down a ladder toward the merchant, lime dust on his shoes; a new gate half built; carts of grey stone; bright dusty day.
A merchant with a boat. Good. Can she carry lead? A church without a roof is a field, and a church without a wall is a gift to the heathen. I am building both.
There is a chest in my school that came home from Daventre with a name written inside the lid, in ink older than I am. My clerks tell me it is the name of your house. I do not forget a lid.
Your ground on the Stathe is pegged. No rent. If a man of mine asks you for any, send him to me, and watch his face.
The king's youngest son is in my school. He is small, and corrects the deacon's Latin. I have told the deacon it is good for him.
The last load was sound. I have another, and it is heavier.
Ask what a name inside a lid is worth
Take his order: six pigs of lead for the roof
Sell him two loads of oak beams (36 d the load)
Look at the walls, and wish him a dry summer
The Vecht side

Three long barges lie nose to tail along a bank faced with old boat planks, and herring barrels are going aboard the last of them. The bishop's toll man sits where the bank meets the Stathe with a tally stick, a token board and a dog.

A long river bank faced with oak posts and weathered ship planks: three flat barges nose to tail, barrels rolling up a gangplank; a toll man on a bench with a tally stick, a board of wooden tokens and a sleeping dog; a lanky boatman leaning on a pole; storehouse doors open to the water, overcast.
The bishop's toll, by King Otto's gift: here, and at Muiden where the Vecht meets the lake. Pay here and I cut you a token for Muiden. Pay there and you pay his cousin, who cannot count.
And what passes is offered on the Stathe first. That is the custom of this bank, and the bank has a long memory and a short temper.
Your house is on my board among the saint's own. No toll. I only count you for the pleasure of it.
I pole the Vecht to Muiden, and the lake to the stream at Medemelacha. Herring up, grain down. My master sold his barge at Easter. I go with the next boat that asks.
You paid without a speech last time. I have put a notch by it. Three notches and I stop looking under the hides.
Pay the toll, and take the token for Muiden
Ask him to look for your house on his board
Hire the Vecht boatman
A plaint at the bishop's mint

The ring of the hammer stops as you pass the mint. A merchant of the Stathe is at the barred window with a handful of thin bright pennies, and your name in his mouth. The moneyer has a scale no bigger than a hand, and he is setting it level.

A small stone room with a barred window inside a town gate: a moneyer holds up a tiny balance with one fat penny in one pan and one thin penny in the other; an angry merchant in a good cloak points through the bars at the viewer; a boy with shears stops cutting to listen; cool shadow, bright street beyond.
He paid me for twelve bolts in these, by count. AMVTHON, it says on them. I counted out a pound and weighed three quarters of one. I say he knew.
Heriman's pennies, from the Ems. Three quarters of what ours weigh, and as good silver as ours. By count they are a short cloak. By weight they are honest. The quarrel is which you used.
Here it is the bishop's penny by count, or any silver by weight. A man who passes light coin by count makes it good, or clears himself by his oath. I hear the oath. I have a good ear for metal.
Your oath rang flat last time. I say so as a man who rings things for his living.
Make the weight good on his own scale (15 d)
Swear you took them by count yourself, in good faith, on the Ems
Ask the moneyer to show you the two weights, and stand the man ale
Adelbold's cathedral
The new church of grey tuff stands where the old Saint Martin's burned, round-arched and higher than anything on the river. Candles burn by the score. A canon at the west door is turning away a pig.

The west door of a tall new Romanesque church of grey tuff with round arches: a canon in a dark cloak shoos a pig off the steps with his sleeve; inside, rows of candles and a high choir; merchants in good cloaks filing in; feast-day morning, banners on the scaffolding of a second church behind.

Hallowed this month before the emperor Henry and twelve bishops. Bishop Adelbold reckoned the round of the apse himself; he has written to a pope about the measure of a ball. We prayed the roof would be simpler.

The emperor Conrad died in this town at Pentecost. His body goes up the Rhine to Speyer. His heart and what lay about it stay here, under a stone in the choir. An emperor in two towns. It will make the reckoning hard at the Last Day.
There is a stone in the choir cut with one word, for the part of an emperor that stayed with us. Pilgrims ask which part. I tell them: the part that was tired.
The saint burns wax like a king. A cake at the altar is remembered at the morning Mass, by name, for a year.
Your house was named at the morning Mass. The merchants' bench looked round to see who it was.
Give a cake of wax at the altar
Sell the canons a cask of wine for the feast (58 d)
Stand at the back through the Mass, among the merchants
The bishop's swallow

The bishop of Traiectum lives in a timber house by Lebuin's church, three days' sail and a lifetime from his own. He is sitting on the threshold with a wax tablet on his knee, looking up at a swallow's nest under the eave. He puts the tablet down when he sees river mud on your shoes.

A timber doorway in morning light, a swallow's nest stuck under the eave: a thin tonsured bishop with ink on his fingers sits on the threshold with a wax tablet, looking up; clerks with a charter chest behind him in the shadow; the merchant in the fenced yard with his cap in his hand.

The merchant. Tell me what the river is doing. My clerks only tell me what the charters are doing. Has Saint Martin's a roof? Does anyone say Mass in it? Begin at the strand and walk me up to the altar.
She nests over my door each spring. I have written her some verses. She is the only one of my flock who comes back on time.
King Zwentibold gave our men here the freedom they had at Dorestad. A dead town's rights, carried up the river like relics. They work as well as relics, I find.
Your house's reckoning is owed to Saint Martin now, they tell me. Then it is owed to a saint in exile, who knows what it is to be short on the day. Ask me for time. Once.
You have been my eyes on that strand. A bishop in exile pays in letters. Mine would say you are the church's man, here and, God willing, at home.
The Life of Lebuin goes forward on your skins. An Englishman, buried among Saxons, written up by a Frank with Frisian blood. The church is like that.
Tell him truly how Traiectum stands, from the strand to the altar
Take his order: two bundles of parchment for the saint's Life
Ask him for time on the house's day
Ask for his letter of protection
Sods and stakes

Where the houses stood there is a black band a hand deep under the new grass. Round it a bank of sods is going up, with a ditch at its foot, and every plot-holder who stayed is carrying. Thiadlef, grey now, sets down his barrow when he sees your boat, and does not smile.

A raw earth rampart curving from a river round a burned settlement, a wet ditch at its foot, split oak stakes along the top: men and women with barrows and hurdles of sods; a lean grey man in a thin blue cloak rests on a barrow handle; a black band of charcoal in the cut bank; cold clear day.
They burned it to the ground, and the ground a hand deep. Where Saint Lebuin rests, the monks will write, as if he had been resting. Now the bishop wants a wall. I am carrying sods at my age.

Every plot owes a stretch: sods, stakes on top, the ditch below. Dig it or pay for it. A stretch that is dug is called by the house's name. A stretch that is paid for is called by the digger's, behind your back.
Dorestad never had a wall. I say that to the young ones when they complain about the barrows.
Your stretch holds. The children have dug charred grain out of the bank below it, and are trying to plant it.
Dig your stretch with the crew: a week of sods
Pay diggers for your stretch (80 d)
Carry sods beside him for a day, plot or no plot
The Hand and the cross

The mint is a strong house inside the wall with one door and a man at it. Inside, a stocky moneyer holds a die in his fist over a block, and strikes once. The new pennies lie in a wooden bowl, pale, with a cross on them. He looks at your purse as other men look at a stranger's dog.

A dim strong-house with one guarded door: a stocky fair moneyer in a leather apron, die in his fist over an oak block, hammer raised; a wooden bowl of pale new pennies, the top one showing a hand coming down out of a cloud; a tiny folding balance on a cord at his neck; hearth glow.
Silver in, pennies out, the king's share off the top. Old coin, foreign coin, broken rings: all one to the fire.
My pennies go north for furs and wax, and I never see one twice. I should like to know what becomes of them. A man likes to hear of his children.
The countess has struck a penny with the English king's Hand on it and our cross behind. I say nothing against it. I have weighed one very carefully. Nobody copies a bad coin.
Now the king's own mint strikes the Hand. So the countess was right, and it is the king who copied her. Do not say I said so.
A penny of mine, cut in half for change and pecked with a knife to see if it bled. I keep thinking of it. I have decided to be flattered.
Tell him where his pennies go: weighed, cut and pecked in the north
Tell the king's man that a die not the king's is being struck
Weigh one of his pennies on your own balance, and say it is true
The weirs at the brook mouth

South of the bank a brook comes in under alders, and two fences of stakes and wattle run across its mouth with basket traps in the gaps. Eels hang smoking on a rack over a slow fire. Herons stand in the shallows and wait their turn, and so does the fisherman.

A brook mouth under alders on a wide brown river: two wattle fences across the water with basket traps, a logboat tied to the last stake; eels hanging on a rack over a low smoky fire; a fisherman squatting on his heels, two herons motionless in the shallows; autumn dusk.
They run to the sea on the dark nights after harvest, and they run through me. Seven pennies the barrel off the rack. On the bank it is ten, and at a lord's table God knows.
The river is a hand lower than at Lammas and will be a man higher by Martinmas. If you mean to lie here the winter, lie on the ridge side.
The first flood took four baskets and a stretch of the lower fence. Stakes I have. Hands I have two of.
The fence you drove is still standing. The heron sits on your stake. He has better manners than my brother-in-law.
Buy two barrels of smoked eels off the rack (14 d)
Lend the crew to drive stakes for an afternoon, for a barrel
Watch the herons, and ask about the river
Lebuin's day

It is the morrow of Martinmas, and the bank has kept two feasts running. The goose is not yet bones. In the church over Lebuin's grave they are singing, the Saxons with the rest, and the smell of roast fat has got in among the wax.

A wooden church on a river dune on a grey November day, its door open and full of people singing; geese roasting on spits outside, children running with drumsticks; a priest in the doorway with a hand bell; the wide brown river running high behind.
Lebuin's day. An Englishman who walked into the Saxons' own assembly and told them a king was coming if they would not hear. They nearly killed him for it, and the king came all the same.
North of the grave and south of the grave they stand, as always. But they are singing the same thing, and a few of them in the same time.
Three times built, twice burned, we used to say: the saint ahead by one. Now it is four times built. He is still ahead.
Bishop Bernold's church has columns like a wood and a vault under it for the saint. The old people say he heard them better through planks.
After today the river goes round us on both sides until spring. An island with ale on it. A man could winter worse.
Keep the feast: goose and ale for the crew (8 d)
Give a cake of wax at the saint's grave
Stand through the Mass, where there is room
The saint's share

On the king's ground a row of oak posts marks off the tenth part that is Saint Martin's. Beside them a sealed bag, a stack of cheeses and four hides are waiting, and the toll man is looking at his own boat as a man looks at a horse that has let him down.

An open piece of river bank with a row of oak posts, a bench and a balance hung from a pole: a long stooped toll man with tally sticks at his belt stands over a sealed bag, stacked cheeses and folded hides, looking at a leaky boat hauled out on the grass; reeds, grey autumn sky.

The saint's tenth goes to Traiectum at Martinmas. I take it myself. My boat leaks. Yours does not. I have counted it twice; the prior will count it twice. Between the two counts it is yours to keep dry.
I have never let it out of my hands. I say so, so that you know what you are being asked.
The prior's stick. Received whole, by your hull. Then here is mine: your boat passes this ground untolled while I sit on this bench. I have cut six such sticks in twenty years.

The prior's stick says eleven cheeses went on to the Almere and ten came off it. I have sailed the Almere. It does not eat cheese. Next year the saint's share goes south in my own boat, leak or no leak.
Take the saint's share aboard for Traiectum
Give him the prior's stick, and take his
Pay him for the cheese, and say no more about it (6 d)
Say your boat is bound the other way
The Dane's balance

The man on the king's ground is big and fair, with a plaited beard and a Frankish cloak. Where the last toll man counted, he takes a folding balance out of a bronze case, and waits for you to put something on it.

The toll ground on a peat-brown stream: a big fair Dane with a plaited beard, a Frankish cloak over a northern tunic and a hacked silver arm ring, holds up a small folding balance; the row of oak posts and a tethered cow behind him; thatched houses, flat grey sky.
A tenth. The king's, the count's, my lord's: call it what you like, it weighs the same. Put it on the pan.
Your Frankish pennies I take by weight. A king can make a coin lighter. He cannot make my balance lie.
The Frisian who does not argue. Sit. I weigh quickly, and then we drink slowly.
You said a penny is a penny. I have thought about it. A penny is a penny in a king's hall. Here it is silver.
The terp men have driven my lord out of the north. He will be back with a king's leave; he always is. But I have begun to think about gorse.
If I am not on this bench next summer, go to the west cliff on Wieringen and look where the gorse is oldest. I say no more, and I did not say that.
Put the tenth on his pan and say nothing
Drink with him when the weighing is done (2 d)
Tell him a penny is a penny, and should be counted
Ask him where a careful man keeps his share
The king's share

A tall spare lord with grey hair cut short, and a sword he wears from habit, is sitting on the toll man's bench with the toll man standing. He asks to see your hands, and then to hear, plainly, what was taken from you here last time.

The toll ground on a peat stream: a tall spare grey-haired lord in a plain dark cloak with a gold pin sits on a rough bench, a sword across his knees, a chaplain behind him; the toll man stands with his tally stick held like a boy caught out; the house row and a small wooden church beyond; mild light.
I hold the king's share of this toll, by his charter. The king is a child and I am not often here. Tell me what the toll man takes, and whether it is what he writes.
The charter gives me toll, mint and rent. I have looked for the mint. There is a bench, a balance and a cow. Clerks write what clerks write.
What I take here I mean for God's use. Saint Martin's at Traiectum wants wax and oil. Bring what the saint needs, and I set my seal to your freedom of this toll.
Count Dirk has his own charter for the land between the two streams, two months younger than mine. We are polite about it. Politeness is cheaper than war, though it takes longer.
The wax came, true weight. I am told so by a monk who does not like merchants, so I believe it.
Tell him plainly what was taken, and what was written
Give two cakes of wax for Saint Martin's
Take his order: four jars of oil for the saint
Ask for his seal on your freedom of the toll
A cross on the bare mound

The island priest has come in by boat and said Mass in the open on the head terp, his back to the weather and his box on the flat stone. Afterwards he walks you to the edge of the second mound, where the old herdsman stands at his square of grass, and stops well short of it.

Two green house mounds in a vast salt marsh: on the nearer a weathered oak cross with a flat stone before it; on the bare second mound an ancient herdsman with a tall pole stands guard by a square of longer grass; between them a weathered priest in a seal-skin cloak talks to the merchant; wind, running cloud.
I want the cross on that mound, not beside it. On my father's island I would have known how to ask. Here he will hear a priest. You he might hear as a man.
Where I was born nobody touched the god's cattle, and water was drawn in silence. I do not scorn it. I came out of it. That is why I want it finished kindly.
He wants to put his post where ours stood. He asks, at least. The last ones weighed the silver on the grass first, and asked nothing.
You told me where the cup went. So I say this to you and not to him: a post is a post. Let him set it at the edge, where the thorn is. Not in the square.
And a roof, one day. I have said Mass in the rain on this terp more often than in the dry. The Lord does not mind. The book does.
Carry the old man's word to the priest: a cross at the edge, by the thorn
Tell the old man the square is the church's ground now
Give toward a roof for the cross (12 d)
Say it is between the two of them, and go down to the boat
Whose boat

Nobody comes down to the creek. From the top of the head mound a heavy-shouldered man watches you make fast, and waits until you have climbed the cattle path before he speaks. There is nothing on him that shines.

The top of a green house mound above a grey tidal creek: a heavy-shouldered man of forty in a plain dark cloak with no brooch, a scar through one eyebrow, a seax at his belt, looks down the cattle path at the merchant climbing; sod houses behind him, sheep, a watch pole; flat hard light.
Whose boat, and who told you to come here? Good. Then come up. We look first, these years.
They burned Westergo from end to end. We were out on the marsh with the sheep. Sods do not burn well. Since then the silver is in the ground, and not on the table.

You are the one who comes back. So: a pot, and a place. Everyone on this mound who knows where could drown in one night. If the house stands empty when you next come, dig it up and take it to my sister's son at Doccinga.
The lord at Dorestad sends for his due. You are a merchant; you know what a place is worth. Has this terp had a good year?
You told them we have sheep. We have sheep. I laughed, afterwards. Ask my wife; it does not happen often.
We have driven the Dane out. Cokingi, they call us in the south. I am digging up what is mine, and I am counting it where you can see.
Let him show you the pot and the place
Say that this terp has sheep, and nothing else
Tell the Dane's counter it has been a very good year
Take the keeper's share he counts out: one penny in twelve
The weaving huts

Three sheds are dug knee-deep into the flank of the mound, their roofs no higher than a standing man. From each comes the knock of a sword beater. The widow who owns the looms looks at your cloak before she looks at you, and is sorry for it.

A sunken weaving hut seen through its low door: an upright loom with rows of clay weights, two women passing a shuttle; in front a small strong widow in grey-blue twill with shears at her belt holds a fold of cloth to the light and frowns at the merchant's cloak; green terp, bright wind.
That is an English cloak, and a poor one. Stand in the light. No: I have seen enough.
A bolt is a winter. Forty-four pennies, and I do not haggle with a winter. At Dorestad they will ask you forty-eight and tell you about the Almere.
My selvedge has a yellow thread in it. If you are ever offered that thread under forty, somebody's door was broken to get it.

My cousin Tetta on the Ems has the best blue on this coast and no red worth the name. I have the red. Carry her a sack of madder from me, and bring back what she sends. We have traded dye by other people's boats for twenty years.
Tetta's woad. She has tied it as if I could not be trusted with string. Give it here. Now: for you the bolt is forty.
Where did the last bolt go? A count's back? A Dane's? I ask everyone. One day somebody will say: a bishop's.
Buy two bolts at her price (88 d)
Take her sack of madder for Tetta on the Ems
Hand over what Tetta sent, and take two bolts at forty (80 d)
Mind the weights, and admire the cloth
The old woman's oath

A clerk from the bishop's house at Traiectum has come north with a writing board, and the whole mound has walked up to the spring to watch. The old woman on the three-legged stool is nearly blind now. She turns her head to your step, and says a second witness has come.

A stone-lined spring on the flank of a church mound: a very old bent woman on a three-legged stool, one hand on a wooden dipper, the other raised flat above her head; a young tonsured clerk kneeling with a wax board; the people of the mound standing round in silence; larks, a wide pale sky.
The bishop wants it written before she dies: what she saw, in her words, sworn. She will swear it before someone who is not of this mound and not of my house. A merchant will do. She said so herself.
I was a child, carrying water. He put the book over his head, so, with both hands. The sword came down on the book. I swear it by this water, and by the church that stands on what they did.
Write it as I said it. Not better.
She says a gospel book. The brothers at Fulda show the book itself, with the cuts in it, and it is no gospel. I shall write what she swears and what Fulda shows, and let the bishop sleep on it.
And I need a hull to Traiectum. The leaves must not get wet, and I must not get drowned, in that order of importance to the bishop.
Stand by, hear her swear, and put your mark under the clerk's
Witness it, and give the clerk passage to Traiectum (16 d)
Say you can swear to what she says, not to what she saw
A board at the Northman's farm

The farm stands on a mound of its own toward the sea, with a boat shed beside the byre and a ship's strake for a lintel. An old man is mending a net by the door with fingers that have held other things. He pushes a board and a bag of pieces toward you with his foot.

A turf-walled farm on its own low mound by the sea, a boat shed beside the byre, a wooden cross nailed over the door: a big white-haired old man in a Frisian farmer's tunic sits on a bench with a net across his knees, pushing a pegged game board forward with his foot; evening, long light, gulls.
A merchant. Good. Merchants bring news and leave. Sit down. Do you play? The king is in the middle and has few men. The others have many, and no king. It is like home.
The cross over the door is mine. The hammer inside it was my father's. I do not ask them to like each other.
Rodulf has been paid on every coast, so he thinks paying is the custom of the country. Where were his ships last seen, and how many? I ask as an old man asks about the weather.
You lost your king in nine moves last time. You guard him too closely. A king who cannot move is taken where he sits.
You beat me. I have told nobody. At my age a man chooses his witnesses.
I will tell you how to know a sail that means harm from one that means trade. It is in the set of the yard, and in how long they look at you before they turn.
Play a game of tafl with him
Tell him where the Danes' ships were last seen
Ask him how to read a sail
Count Bruno's pennies

On the long mound a small plank house has a barred door, and a boy sweeping its floor into a pan. Inside two men strike in turn. Each blow leaves a thin bright penny with a crowned head on it, and the name of a count nobody here has seen.

A small plank mint on a terp: an anvil set in an oak stump, two men striking in turn, a neat small moneyer in a leather apron with a folding scale at his belt holding a thin bright penny to the light of the barred door; a boy sweeping silver dust into a pan; market booths outside.
Silver? Lay it there. Do not tell me what it weighs. The scale has not heard you and will not agree.
DOCC on one side, BRVN on the other, and the king's head. I am told the count is a tall man. I only know his name fits the die.
A skipper took four hundred of mine east last spring. Beyond the Baltic they cut them in half to make change. Half my work, he said, and laughed.
The count is dead on the road, they say, killed. I strike his name until someone brings me a new one. A penny does not mourn.
The merchant with the honest bag. Or the careful one. I have not yet decided which.
Bring me your old and foreign silver first, and I strike it at my own count: the count's due, and nothing for my trouble.
Have a pound of mixed silver struck into his pennies (the count's due: 8 d)
Take up his offer: your silver struck at his own count
Ask where his pennies go
Corn for the north

Folcger is on the creek bank before your plank is down, looking at the water. A hull lies further up the creek with her mast lowered. He has seen what you carry by how you sit, and he has a price to say that is not the mound's price.

A muddy creek under a low green mound: a short broad ferryman with a sounding pole looks at the water, not at the merchant; further up the creek a dark clinker hull with her mast lowered; on the mound above a lean woman with blue-stained forearms watches with her arms folded; dusk.

There is hunger north of the Eider too, and silver. The hull in the creek gives nine pennies the sack for rye, by weight, tonight, and asks to see no measure. The mound gives you cloth and a blessing.

The emperor's law this year: no food sold out of the realm while there is hunger in it. I know the law. I stood in the ring when it was read. This creek is where the realm stops, and it stops a little short of that hull.

He has told you what the Danes pay. I tell you what we pay: a bolt of blue for four sacks, and my daughter eats. I do not say which is the better trade. I say you will be asked, some day, which you made.
Sell four sacks of rye over the side to the north-bound hull (36 d)
Sell the four sacks on the mound, for a bolt of blue
Tell Folcger your corn is spoken for
The house with the looms

The house is three paces wide, with two looms against the long wall and the clay weights swinging. A pot of barley and mutton is on the fire. Tetta counts your crew as they stoop in at the door, and moves the pot nearer the edge.

The inside of a narrow plank house: two upright looms with swinging clay weights against the long wall, a fire on the floor with a pot, sleeping benches under hung cloaks; a lean woman with forearms blue to the elbow ladles into bowls while four boatmen stoop in at the low door; warm smoky light.
You eat here, you sleep here, and we talk about cloth in the morning. That is the order of things on this mound.
Blue is forty-four the bolt. My arms are that colour to the elbow, so you know it is not bought dye.
Liafburg's madder. She has sewn the sack shut twice. She thinks the whole coast is after her red. Sit: I will make up the woad, and a word for her that you need not understand.
Nobody has yet asked me whose shoes stood by my door in the year of the rising. Somebody will. I should like it to be a man who did not see them.
Your bench is as you left it. So is what you owe me for the ale: nothing. I looked.
Buy two bolts of her blue (88 d)
Give her Liafburg's madder, and take the woad back west
Eat at her fire, and sleep on the bench
Heriman's die

By the count's post stands a locked plank house, and today the door is open: a block with an iron die in it, a man with a hammer, a boy shearing a silver sheet into rounds. The moneyer's wife is leaning in the doorway with dye-black fingers, and names your forefathers before she names a price.

The open door of a small plank mint on a terp street: a round-faced woman in a dark blue gown with a silver penny on a cord at her neck leans on the door post; behind her a moneyer at a block with a die, a boy with shears and a silver sheet; thin crooked pennies in a bowl; a post with a horse's skull outside.
My husband gives five of ours for four of Tiel's, and smiles. Ours say Heriman and Amuthon. They are light, yes. They are also here, which the Tiel ones are not.
By count: the shepherds, the count's toll, the little markets along this coast. By weight: Daventre, Tiel, every Dane. Know which bank you stand on before you open the bag.

A house from the Rhine mouth sold corn on this mound at a fair price in a hungry year, before there was a church. My mother's mothers said so, eight of them. We keep cloth back for that house. It is owed.
Four houses on the street went in one night. We passed the dies out through the wall before we passed the children. I am not proud of the order.
The bench you are sitting on has been mended twice since your people first sat on it. It is the same bench. We are that kind of house.
Take the cloth that is owed to your house
Have him weigh a Tiel penny against one of his, and learn the two weights
Change twenty heavy pennies for twenty-five of his, to spend along the coast
Sit on the mended bench, and hear the mound's news
Whose pennies

At the head of the creek stands a post with a horse's skull on it, and under it a man in a Westphalian cloak with a tally stick. He counts your bales up the plank, and then asks a thing that is not about bales.

The head of a muddy creek below a terp: a post with a horse's skull, a bench, a man in a heavy Westphalian cloak notching a tally stick while porters carry bales up a plank; a dog at his feet; across the wide river, far off, the smoke of another market; raw spring light.

The archbishop of Bremen has a mint and a market over the river now, and wants this one. My lord the count has the post. So I ask every skipper, and I notch the answers: in whose pennies would you rather be paid?
It is only a stick. But sticks are read aloud, at the end, by whoever is left holding the post.
The king has ordered the county handed over. The archbishop has sent a man to take it. My lord has not yet found the time to give it up.
You said the count's pennies when it cost nothing. Say it again, now that it does.
Say: the count's pennies, here, as your fathers were paid
Say it again, before the archbishop's man
Say: the archbishop's, since the king's parchment says so
Say: in silver, by weight, and let lords settle the names
Godfred, king of the Danes, has been killed by one of his own following. His two hundred ships have left the Frisian islands, and his brother's son Hemming asks the emperor for peace.
King Cnut is dead and lies at Winchester. His sons share his kingdoms between them, and the English do not yet know which of them is their king.
Count Bruno's thin pennies from Doccinga pass by count on the Frisian coast and by weight everywhere else. Beyond the Baltic they are cut in half for small change.
